meta.title: onsemi (ON Semiconductor): Hassane El-Khoury's Pivot from Commodity Components to Intelligent Power — How Silicon Carbide, ADAS Image Sensors, and the Treo Analog Platform Repositioned a Legacy Motorola Spinout as the Infrastructure Backbone of EV Electrification and AI Data Centers
meta.abstract: ON Semiconductor Corporation — operating as onsemi since 2021 — is a Scottsdale, Arizona-based semiconductor company that has undergone one of the most consequential strategic transformations in the industry over the 2020–2025 period. Founded in 1999 as a leveraged buyout of Motorola's Semiconductor Components Group, the company spent its first two decades as a broad-based supplier of commodity discrete components and analog ICs. The arrival of CEO Hassane El-Khoury in December 2020, recruited from Cypress Semiconductor (where he had orchestrated a similar high-value pivot before its sale to Infineon), marked a decisive inflection. El-Khoury rapidly rationalized the product portfolio, exited non-strategic businesses including the Quantenna Wi-Fi division, and concentrated R&D and capital expenditure on three high-value vectors: silicon carbide (SiC) power semiconductors for EV traction inverters and onboard chargers, complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensors for automotive ADAS and machine vision, and a proprietary analog and mixed-signal platform branded Treo — a 65nm BCD process capable of 1–90V operation at 175°C. The 2021 acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies (GTAT) for $415 million secured vertical integration in SiC crystal growth, enabling onsemi to internally produce 150mm and emerging 200mm boules and wafers. By 2023 onsemi's SiC revenue had crossed $1 billion, representing approximately 25% global market share and the fastest dollar-growth in the industry. Full-year 2025 revenue settled at $5.995 billion — down from a $8.25 billion peak in 2023 as the automotive inventory correction and EV demand softening compressed volumes — yet the company generated a record $1.42 billion in free cash flow (24% margin) and returned 100% of that to shareholders via buybacks. As of Q1 2026, sequential momentum has returned: AI data-center revenue grew more than 30% quarter-over-quarter, gross margin expanded for the third consecutive quarter to 38.5%, and management guided FY2026 AI revenue above $500 million on a path to doubling year-over-year. This dossier evaluates onsemi across its strategic transformation thesis, financial architecture, competitive positioning versus STMicroelectronics, Infineon, and Wolfspeed, and the 12- to 60-month outlook as electrification and AI infrastructure converge.

chapters.title: The Power Architect: onsemi at the Intersection of Electrification and AI
chapters.body:
In the spring of 2026, onsemi's quarterly results offered what its investors had been waiting nearly three years to see: a trough that looked genuinely like a trough. First-quarter revenue of $1,513 million came in ahead of guidance, non-GAAP gross margin expanded for the third consecutive quarter — reaching 38.5% — and revenue from artificial-intelligence data centres surged more than 30% sequentially. When management guided second-quarter 2026 revenue to a midpoint of $1,590 million, the contours of a recovery were unmistakable. The painful 27% decline from the company's $8.25 billion peak in 2023 to the $5,995.4 million trough of 2025 had, it appeared, run its course.

That trough had arrived while onsemi was executing perhaps the most consequential industrial repositioning in the power semiconductor industry since the 2010s — a pivot timed, deliberately or not, to coincide with three secular forces reshaping the global energy and technology infrastructure.

## Three Forces, One Portfolio

The first is the electrification of transportation. Every EV traction inverter must convert battery power into rotational force across 400V and 800V architectures that conventional silicon cannot efficiently serve. Silicon carbide power semiconductors — specifically SiC MOSFETs rated at 650V and 1200V, sold under onsemi's EliteSiC brand — are the enabling technology. Each EV that displaces an internal combustion vehicle represents a step-function increase in SiC content per unit; each 800V platform that replaces a 400V predecessor demands more capable, and more expensively priced, silicon carbide.

The second force is the proliferation of ADAS sensing. A contemporary vehicle may carry eight to twelve cameras for lane-keeping, object detection, and driver monitoring — a number that grows as regulators and insurers embed ADAS requirements into safety ratings. Each camera requires a high-dynamic-range CMOS image sensor engineered to perform across temperature extremes and rapidly shifting illumination. onsemi is the largest automotive image sensor supplier in the world, a position established through long design-win cycles at tier-1 camera module integrators that translate into multiyear revenue predictability across successive platform generations.

The third force is the power density problem inside AI data centres. A rack of GPUs training a large language model draws many times the power of conventional server infrastructure. Delivering that power efficiently at 48-volt distribution levels requires the kind of high-frequency, low-loss switching that only wide-bandgap semiconductors can provide. In January 2025, onsemi expanded its wide-bandgap coverage by acquiring Qorvo's SiC JFET technology for $118.8 million — a topology particularly suited to the AC-DC conversion stage in AI server power supply units where switching frequency and efficiency density are critical design constraints. AI data-centre revenue grew more than 30% sequentially in Q1 2026; management guided the segment above $500 million for full-year 2026.

## The Architect

The executive who repositioned onsemi to serve all three vectors simultaneously was Hassane El-Khoury, who joined as President and CEO in December 2020 after leading Cypress Semiconductor through a strategic transformation that culminated in Infineon Technologies' $9.5 billion acquisition of the company in April 2020. His playbook at onsemi has been a faithful enlargement of the Cypress model: exit low-margin commodity lines without sentiment, concentrate capital on differentiated automotive and industrial platforms, and lock in long-term supply agreements that reduce revenue volatility and justify ongoing manufacturing investment. The practical execution included abandoning the Wi-Fi chipset business acquired with Quantenna Communications, rebranding the company from ON Semiconductor to onsemi in 2021, and completing the $415 million acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies — a New Hampshire crystal grower that management described as "the final piece" of a fully vertically integrated SiC supply chain spanning crystal growth, wafer slicing, epitaxial deposition, and device fabrication.

## The Financial Benchmark

The trough of that transformation produced an instructive paradox. [Full-year 2025 revenue of $5,995.4 million](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0) sat 27% below the 2023 peak, yet onsemi generated non-GAAP free cash flow of $1,418.6 million — a 24% margin — and returned the entirety of it to shareholders through buybacks. A business selling differentiated automotive-grade semiconductors under long-term supply agreements had, it turned out, a materially different cost structure than the commodity component manufacturer that Motorola had spun out in 1999.

| | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Q2 2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $8,252.4M | $7,082.3M | $5,995.4M | $1,590M midpoint |
| Non-GAAP Gross Margin | — | — | 38.4% | — |
| Non-GAAP FCF / Margin | — | — | $1,418.6M / 24.0% | — |

## The Central Question

The dossier that follows examines whether the competitive advantages El-Khoury assembled — a vertically integrated SiC supply chain anchored in GTAT's crystal growth capabilities, global leadership in automotive image sensors accumulated through years of design-win incumbency, and the Treo proprietary 65nm BCD analog platform that allows onsemi to capture margin on application-specific ICs rather than competing on commodity catalog pricing — constitute durable structural moats. Or whether they represent a first-mover advantage in markets so large and lucrative that better-capitalised rivals — STMicroelectronics, Infineon, and Chinese domestic SiC producers now scaling behind protective procurement relationships with NEV OEMs — will erode the economics before onsemi can establish the scale and customer lock-in that would make the pivot irreversible.

chapters.title: The Long Road from Motorola's Basement: ON Semiconductor's 27-Year Arc
chapters.body:
## Origin Story: The Motorola Divestiture, August 1999

The semiconductor that ON Semiconductor was born to make had a name that said everything about its ambitions: jellybean. Zener diodes, small-signal transistors, rectifiers, voltage regulators — the unremarkable but essential building blocks that sat in billions of circuit boards without ever commanding a premium. On August 4, 1999, Texas Pacific Group completed a $1.6 billion leveraged recapitalization of Motorola's Semiconductor Components Group, spinning out a company whose founding identity was inseparable from the commodity economics of the components it sold.

The spinout inherited seven wafer-fabrication facilities, 22 assembly and test plants, approximately 22,000 employees, and a customer proposition that was explicitly about simplicity: OEMs could consolidate their discrete component vendors and deal with a single, reliable, low-cost source. Steve Hanson, a career Motorola executive, was appointed founding CEO. Motorola retained a minority stake. Eight months later, in April 2000, the company listed on NASDAQ under the ticker ON — at the precise moment semiconductor valuations peaked — raising capital intended primarily to service the leveraged capital structure it had inherited rather than to fund research into the differentiated technologies that would define the industry's next quarter-century.

The IPO timing was, in retrospect, a portent of the decade ahead.

## A Decade of Bolt-On Accumulation, 2001–2015

The years between the dot-com bust and the Obama administration produced a company whose strategic logic was consolidation rather than transformation. Keith Jackson, who succeeded Hanson and ran the company from 2002 through 2020, oversaw a disciplined if unspectacular program of acquisitions that broadened onsemi's analog and mixed-signal portfolio without fundamentally disturbing its commodity positioning.

AMIS Holdings arrived in 2008, adding application-specific integrated circuits and custom mixed-signal capabilities aimed at the medical and industrial markets. Catalyst Semiconductor followed in 2010, strengthening the EEPROM and non-volatile memory offering. The 2011 acquisition of Sanyo Semiconductor was the largest of this era, a roughly $400 million transaction that added manufacturing depth across Japan and South Korea — Aizu assembly sites that remain part of the operational footprint to this day — along with expanded coverage in image sensors and automotive components that would prove, years later, to have been seeds planted in more fertile soil than anyone then recognized.

Throughout this period, the financial profile was characteristic of a company whose products were bought on price. Gross margins fluctuated in the low-to-mid thirties. Debt management consumed significant executive attention. Revenue grew by acquisition more than by organic innovation. The company was profitable, solvent, and widely considered a workmanlike but uninspiring participant in the middle tier of the power semiconductor market.

## The Fairchild Acquisition, 2016: The Hinge Point Nobody Recognized in Real Time

What the annual reports from 2016 described as a power-management consolidation play now reads, with the benefit of hindsight, as the single transaction that made everything that followed structurally possible.

In September 2016, following a competitive process that had drawn interest from multiple bidders including China Resources Microelectronics, ON Semiconductor closed its $2.4 billion acquisition of Fairchild Semiconductor — the largest deal in the company's history and the largest power semiconductor acquisition of that decade. Fairchild brought insulated-gate bipolar transistors, silicon carbide device research, intelligent power modules, and a decades-deep applications engineering heritage in power conversion that the jellybean-era ON Semiconductor had never possessed.

The integration was difficult. Fairchild's manufacturing footprint overlapped with ON's in ways that required years of rationalization. Cultural friction between the two organizations slowed synergy realization. But technically, the acquisition deposited into ON Semiconductor's product library the IGBT expertise, the SiC device process knowledge, and the power module manufacturing capability that Hassane El-Khoury would, four years later, identify as the platform on which to build something entirely different. The Fairchild deal was, in the language of geology, the substrate layer — the formation that made later growth possible without itself being visible at the surface.

## The Transition Years, 2019–2020

Keith Jackson's final years as CEO were marked by continued acquisitions — most notably the June 2019 purchase of Quantenna Communications for approximately $1 billion, adding Wi-Fi 6E chipsets for connected-home applications — and by a growing divergence between the markets ON Semiconductor was positioning toward and the financial profile those markets actually required. Quantenna's customer base was consumer-facing and volume-dependent. The gross margin structure it carried was incompatible with the automotive and industrial franchise that some within the company had begun to argue was the only defensible long-term positioning.

El-Khoury's arrival in December 2020, following a stint as President and CEO of Cypress Semiconductor — which he had sold to Infineon for $9.5 billion in April 2020 — brought immediate and unmistakable clarity of purpose. Within weeks of taking the role, he communicated to analysts and investors a framework that had no precedent in ON Semiconductor's history: the company would exit commoditized product lines, reduce SKU count by hundreds, concentrate capital on automotive and industrial applications, and pursue margin expansion as a primary objective even at the cost of near-term revenue. The message was, in effect, that the company had been optimizing the wrong variable for twenty years.

## The 2021 Pivot: Rebranding, Vertical Integration, and Deliberate Destruction

The year 2021 was the pivot made visible. In November, onsemi — the company dropped the "ON Semiconductor" name alongside the upper case, the lowercase logotype a calculated signal of departure from commodity heritage — completed the $415 million acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies, a Nashua, New Hampshire manufacturer of silicon carbide crystal boules and wafers. Management described GTAT as the final piece of a fully vertically integrated SiC supply chain spanning crystal growth, wafer slicing and polishing, epitaxial deposition, and device fabrication. In an industry where SiC substrate shortages had historically been the rate-limiting constraint on competitors' ability to ramp production, controlling the crystal upstream was not merely an operational efficiency — it was a structural moat.

Also in 2021, El-Khoury shut down the Quantenna division. The business had failed to find a strategic buyer. Rather than maintain a dilutive operation within the portfolio, management wrote off the approximately $1 billion investment and redeployed the capital. The deliberateness of this destruction was the message: a CEO willing to absorb a $1 billion impairment to maintain strategic coherence was not going to be argued out of the portfolio transformation by quarterly earnings pressure.

## Building the Three Pillars, 2022–2025

The SiC revenue ramp that followed was among the fastest in the company's history. By 2023, onsemi's SiC business exceeded $1 billion in annual revenue, anchored by supply agreements that included a disclosed $1.9 billion, 10-year contract with Vitesco Technologies and strategic partnerships with Volkswagen Group and BMW for next-generation EV traction inverter architectures. The Intelligent Sensing Group — inheritor of the image sensor work that Sanyo had seeded — grew alongside it, with onsemi establishing itself as the largest automotive image sensor supplier globally, serving ADAS camera stacks across surround-view, forward-facing perception, and driver monitoring applications.

| Milestone | Year | Value |
|---|---|---|
| TPG leveraged buyout (Motorola spinout) | 1999 | $1.6B recapitalization |
| NASDAQ IPO | 2000 | — |
| Fairchild Semiconductor acquisition | 2016 | $2.4B |
| Quantenna Communications acquisition | 2019 | ~$1.0B |
| El-Khoury appointed CEO | Dec 2020 | — |
| GTAT (SiC crystal) acquisition | Nov 2021 | $415M |
| Quantenna shutdown | 2022 | ~$1.0B write-off |
| SiC revenue crosses $1B | 2023 | — |
| Qorvo SiC JFET acquisition | Jan 2025 | $118.8M |
| Treo analog platform launch | Late 2024 | — |
| $6B buyback authorization | Nov 2025 | Over 3 years |

The 2023 revenue peak of $8.25 billion gave way to correction. An industry-wide automotive semiconductor inventory digestion cycle through 2024 and into 2025 pulled total revenue to approximately $6 billion, a 15% decline from the prior year's $7.08 billion. But the downcycle revealed something the pre-transformation company had never demonstrated: cost discipline durable enough to generate $1.42 billion in free cash flow on a $6 billion revenue base. That figure — record free cash flow at a revenue level that would previously have produced much thinner margins — was the clearest evidence that the business had structurally changed, not merely cyclically recovered.

The Qorvo SiC JFET acquisition in January 2025, at $118.8 million, extended the EliteSiC portfolio into a device topology optimized for the high-frequency switching demands of AI data-center power supply units — the earliest visible signal of a third growth vector taking shape alongside automotive and sensing. By early 2026, that vector had become explicit: management guided AI data-center revenue above $500 million for the full year, implying roughly 100% year-over-year growth on the back of Q1 sequential acceleration exceeding 30%.

Twenty-seven years after Texas Pacific Group carved a commodity components manufacturer out of Motorola's industrial operations in a $1.6 billion leveraged transaction, the company that emerged was supplying the power infrastructure of electric vehicles, autonomous perception systems, and the GPU clusters remaking the global computing industry. The jellybean era had ended.

chapters.title: Platforms and Products: SiC, Image Sensing, and the Treo Analog Ecosystem
chapters.body:
## The Power Solutions Group: Wide-Bandgap Physics as Competitive Moat

Silicon carbide's commercial appeal in power electronics derived from a physical reality that silicon could not overcome. Where conventional silicon loses efficiency as blocking voltage and operating temperature rise — a consequence of its 1.1 eV bandgap and relatively poor thermal conductivity — silicon carbide's 3.26 eV bandgap allowed it to block voltages three to ten times higher, conduct heat roughly three times more effectively, and switch at frequencies that would destroy a comparable silicon device. In practical terms, an SiC MOSFET in an electric vehicle traction inverter dissipated significantly less energy as heat, enabling either a smaller cooling system, a higher peak power output, or a measurable improvement in range at equivalent battery capacity. These properties explained why automotive engineers specifying 400V and 800V traction architectures in 2023 and 2024 overwhelmingly preferred SiC over silicon IGBTs, and why onsemi's Power Solutions Group became the company's most strategically contested business unit.

The PSG's flagship product family, marketed under the **EliteSiC** brand, spanned 650V and 1200V MOSFETs targeting the full EV powertrain stack: traction inverters, onboard chargers, and DC-DC converters. The 1200V devices addressed the high-voltage architectures increasingly favored by European and Korean OEMs seeking faster charging and lower copper weight in harnesses. EliteSiC MOSFETs competed directly against STMicroelectronics' SiC MOSFET line — the market leader with roughly 35% share — and Infineon's CoolSiC product family, both of which had announced parallel capacity expansions through 2025 and 2026.

What separated onsemi's market position from a purely product-level comparison was the supply chain architecture assembled between 2021 and 2025. The November 2021 acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies (GTAT) for $415 million gave onsemi ownership of SiC crystal boule and wafer production at the Hudson, New Hampshire facility — the highest-lead-time, most supply-constrained input in the entire SiC manufacturing chain. Crystal growth, wafer slicing, epitaxial deposition, and device fabrication at the East Fishkill, New York 200mm fab together formed a vertically integrated sequence that neither STMicroelectronics nor Infineon fully replicated. Management described GTAT as "the final piece" of a supply chain that shielded onsemi's production commitments from the external wafer shortages that had periodically throttled competitors' shipments.

In January 2025 onsemi extended the EliteSiC portfolio beyond MOSFETs by acquiring Qorvo's silicon carbide JFET technology business for $118.8 million. The JFET topology offered distinct switching characteristics at high frequencies — particularly relevant for the AC-DC conversion front end of AI data-center power supply units, where engineers were demanding switching frequencies and efficiency densities that strained conventional MOSFET designs. The acquisition added a complementary device topology without requiring a new fabrication investment, effectively doubling the number of circuit topologies onsemi could address with wide-bandgap silicon carbide.

The wide-bandgap roadmap did not stop at SiC. In 2026, onsemi announced a portfolio of vertical gallium nitride (vGaN) devices, which offered superior performance below approximately 900V and at higher switching frequencies than SiC could efficiently sustain. Concurrently, a memorandum of understanding with Innoscience — a specialist lateral GaN foundry — signaled onsemi's intent to access GaN-on-silicon capacity through a foundry relationship rather than owned capital, preserving balance-sheet flexibility while extending the wide-bandgap product catalog.

## The Analog and Mixed-Signal Group: Treo as Vertical Integration in Analog

onsemi's Analog and Mixed-Signal Group carried a different strategic burden than PSG. Where the SiC business required manufacturing scale and substrate supply, the AMG's challenge was architectural: the company historically sourced standard catalog analog components — voltage regulators, power management ICs, interface chips — from third-party suppliers including Texas Instruments and Microchip Technology, foregoing the margin that accrues to the analog IC designer. The Treo platform, launched in late 2024, was designed to change that structure.

Treo was built on a 65-nanometer bulk CMOS process augmented with drain-extended DMOS (BCD) transistors — a process node that allowed the coexistence of dense digital logic, precision analog circuits, and high-voltage power devices on a single die. The operating envelope of 1 to 90 volts and junction temperatures to 175 degrees Celsius covered the full specification range demanded by automotive grade-one components, from 12V body electronics to 48V mild-hybrid power converters and 90V industrial motor interfaces.

The platform's modularity was its central commercial proposition. A common process node and shared design library allowed AMG engineers to generate derivative product families — a new LED driver topology, a multi-phase controller variant, a different LDO architecture — without requalifying the process from scratch for each. Initial Treo product families shipped to customers included ultrasonic sensors for automotive park-assist and in-cabin gesture-recognition, ultra-low-power analog front-ends, LDO regulators, multi-phase PWM controllers for server and EV battery management applications, automotive LED drivers, and single-pair Ethernet controllers conforming to the IEEE 802.3cg standard increasingly adopted in vehicle zonal architectures. Teledyne Technologies publicly disclosed selection of the Treo platform for advanced infrared imaging system design, providing an early third-party validation.

The strategic logic was direct: by owning the analog process node and the derivative IP generated on it, onsemi could price its SiC power modules, image sensor camera subsystems, and analog interface chips as integrated bills of materials rather than as individual components competing on catalog price. The margin captured at each layer of the stack — crystal, wafer, device, and now analog IC — compounded across the full automotive sensor-fusion or EV powertrain design win.

## The Intelligent Sensing Group: Global Market Leadership in Automotive Vision

By the time El-Khoury began restructuring onsemi's portfolio in earnest, the Intelligent Sensing Group already occupied an enviable market position: the company was the largest supplier of automotive CMOS image sensors globally, an installed base advantage accumulated through years of design-win cycles at tier-1 camera module suppliers and ADAS platform integrators. The ISG's product catalog as of 2025 addressed the full range of automotive and industrial machine-vision requirements.

The core of ISG's automotive revenue derived from CMOS image sensors spanning 1 megapixel to 8 megapixels, covering surround-view cameras, front-facing ADAS perception, driver-monitoring systems, and rear-view camera modules. These sensors were manufactured at the South Portland, Maine wafer fabrication facility. The product families offered both global-shutter and rolling-shutter readout architectures: global shutter captured all pixels simultaneously, eliminating motion artifacts critical for high-speed object detection, while rolling shutter offered a cost and power advantage for lower-speed applications. High dynamic range (HDR) capability — the ability to resolve detail simultaneously in bright headlight glare and shadowed road surfaces — was a mandatory specification across ADAS camera platforms by 2024.

ISG's product reach extended beyond conventional visible-spectrum imaging. The short-wave infrared (SWIR) sensor line — sensitive to wavelengths between roughly 900 and 1700 nanometers — addressed industrial inspection applications where silicon-based detectors were blind: semiconductor wafer defect detection, pharmaceutical tablet inspection, food sorting systems, and solar cell quality control. Separately, the silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) portfolio served as the receiver module in LiDAR systems employing direct time-of-flight (dToF) ranging, counting individual photons reflected from target surfaces to reconstruct three-dimensional point clouds at extended range. Single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) arrays complemented this offering for shorter-range depth-sensing in robotics and consumer lidar applications. Together, the SiPM and SPAD lines connected ISG to the autonomous-vehicle LiDAR stack without requiring onsemi to manufacture the full LiDAR unit, capturing the high-value detector component while leaving system integration to specialist vendors.

## Technology Risks and Competitive Exposure

Each of the three product pillars carried distinct competitive vulnerabilities that the company's own disclosures and management commentary acknowledged. In image sensing, Sony's automotive sensor ambitions represented the most acute threat: Sony Semiconductor Solutions held leading positions in smartphone camera sensors and had publicly committed to expanding into automotive-grade image sensing with the engineering depth and process sophistication of a tier-one consumer electronics supplier. Samsung's sensor division posed a parallel risk in the mid-resolution automotive tier. onsemi's lead in global-shutter architecture and its installed base with ADAS platform integrators provided near-term protection, but the long-term competitive dynamics were not settled.

In SiC, the pace of onsemi's 200mm wafer transition relative to STMicroelectronics and Infineon was the central execution risk. STMicroelectronics had announced its own 200mm SiC wafer roadmap and was committed to internal substrate supply through a joint venture with Soitec. Infineon's CoolSiC ramp at its Villach, Austria fab targeted similar production timescales. If onsemi's East Fishkill 200mm conversion ran behind schedule while competitors achieved volume production sooner, the yield and cost advantages the company projected from the transition could be delayed or partially eroded. Chinese domestic SiC producers — several of which had disclosed aggressive capacity expansion plans targeting home-market NEV OEMs — represented an additional price-pressure vector in onsemi's fastest-growing customer geography.

The Treo platform's differentiation relative to Texas Instruments' and Microchip's established automotive analog portfolios was the third open question. Texas Instruments had accumulated decades of process know-how and an enormous catalog of application-specific analog ICs across automotive power management. Treo's initial product families were competitively narrow; the platform's value would ultimately be validated by the breadth and volume of derivative products that AMG engineers could generate from the common process node over a multi-year roadmap.

## Roadmap: 200mm SiC, Treo Extensions, and the Data-Center Power Expansion

Management's stated priorities for 2026 and beyond centered on three parallel ramps. The 200mm SiC wafer production transition at East Fishkill represented the highest-stakes near-term manufacturing execution objective: larger wafer diameter reduces the per-die substrate cost substantially and is the primary lever for closing the unit economics gap between SiC and silicon in cost-sensitive applications. Volume production on 200mm was targeted to scale meaningfully through 2026 and into 2027, with GTAT's crystal growth operations in Hudson providing the internal substrate supply to insulate the ramp from external wafer constraints.

The Treo platform was expected to generate additional product family launches through 2026, extending the initial catalog of ultrasonic sensors and multi-phase controllers into further automotive and industrial applications. AMG's internal roadmap prioritized derivative products that could attach to existing SiC or image-sensor design wins — effectively filling the analog signal chain within already-won platform architectures.

Perhaps most significant for the revenue mix beyond automotive, onsemi's AI data-center power business had grown more than 30% sequentially in Q1 2026, and management guided the segment above $500 million for the full fiscal year — implying roughly 100% year-over-year growth from a base that had scarcely existed eighteen months earlier. The combination of EliteSiC MOSFETs, the newly acquired JFET topology, and Treo's multi-phase controllers positioned PSG and AMG jointly to address 48V rack power conversion architectures being specified across hyperscaler GPU cluster builds. If the automotive inventory correction of 2025 had illustrated the risk of single-market concentration, the AI data-center ramp offered onsemi a second large-scale growth vector that operated on a different demand cycle — one driven by capital expenditure commitments at infrastructure hyperscalers rather than by consumer vehicle purchase decisions.

chapters.title: The Numbers Behind the Transformation: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and Capital Structure
chapters.body:
The revenue arc that Hassane El-Khoury inherited in late 2020 and then bent toward structural growth tells most of the story before a single margin line is examined. In fiscal year 2019, the year before his arrival, ON Semiconductor generated approximately $5.5 billion in revenue — a sum that adequately described its standing as a manufacturer of broadly useful but undifferentiated components, a company that grew when electronics cycles grew and contracted when they did. By fiscal 2023, after three years of strategic redirection, vertical integration investment in silicon carbide, and a deliberate exit from commodity product lines, revenue had risen to [$8.252 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001097864/000109786426000006/on-20251231.htm) — a figure that overstated the sustainable earnings power of the business because it was amplified by the automotive semiconductor supercycle and the inventory-building behavior of tier-1 suppliers caught short during COVID-era supply disruptions. The correction that followed was sharp: [$7.082 billion in fiscal 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001097864/000109786426000006/on-20251231.htm) and then [$5.995 billion in fiscal 2025](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0) as the same tier-1 customers who had built excess inventory worked it down through extended order pauses. The depth of the correction was painful. Its floor, however, was not 2019.

## From Supercycle Peak to Cyclical Trough

The distance between the $8.252 billion peak in fiscal 2023 and the $5.995 billion trough in fiscal 2025 — a $2.26 billion decline, or roughly 27% — obscures the structural story. In 2019, before the transformation, onsemi's revenue base reflected the commodity pricing dynamics of standard jellybean components: margins were thin, switching costs were low, and revenue tracked end-market volumes with few differentiated buffers. By 2025, even at the trough, the company's revenue floor sat approximately 60% above that pre-transformation level. The operational drivers of the 2024–2025 decline were specific and transitory: automotive semiconductor distributors and tier-1 suppliers had over-indexed on SiC and mixed-signal inventory as EV OEMs revised their production build plans downward in response to slower-than-projected consumer adoption and intensifying price competition from Chinese NEV manufacturers. This was not onsemi losing share; it was onsemi's customers working through stock they had already purchased. The distinction matters for interpreting the recovery.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | YoY Change | Primary Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2019 | ~$5,500M | — | Pre-transformation commodity base |
| FY2023 | $8,252M | Supercycle peak | Automotive ramp, SiC design wins |
| FY2024 | $7,082M | –14.2% | Inventory digestion begins |
| FY2025 | $5,995M | –15.3% | Extended EV demand revision |
| Q4 2025 | $1,530M | Stabilization | Inventory clearing |
| Q1 2026 | $1,513M | Recovery base | AI datacenter acceleration |

The sequential quarterly data confirmed the inflection by late 2025. After reaching a trough near $1,450 million in mid-2025, [revenue stabilized at $1,530.1 million in the fourth quarter](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0). The company entered fiscal 2026 with [Q1 revenue of $1,513 million](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-first-quarter-2026-gs4gw3jyioon) — slightly below the Q4 level but ahead of guidance midpoints — before management issued Q2 2026 guidance of $1,540 million to $1,640 million. Annualizing the $1,590 million midpoint implies a revenue run-rate approaching $6.36 billion, squarely within the sell-side consensus range of $6.3 to $6.5 billion for the full year, and substantially above the 2019 pre-transformation baseline.

## The Margin Architecture: GAAP, Non-GAAP, and the 530-Basis-Point Gap

The most instructive financial narrative in onsemi's 2025 annual results is not the revenue decline but the durability of gross margin through it. On a non-GAAP basis, [full-year gross margin for fiscal 2025 was 38.4%](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0), the lowest quarterly reading having been approximately 37.6% in the second quarter before recovering. That range — 37.6% to 38.5% in the worst revenue year since El-Khoury's arrival — compares to a pre-transformation non-GAAP gross margin range of approximately 33% to 35%. The 300-to-500-basis-point structural improvement in the margin floor is the quantified consequence of product mix migration: automotive-grade SiC MOSFETs and CMOS image sensors carry materially higher average selling prices and switching costs than standard rectifiers and voltage regulators.

The reported [GAAP gross margin of 33.1%](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001097864/000109786426000006/on-20251231.htm) in fiscal 2025 told a different story, one that investors and management set aside in favor of the non-GAAP figure. The approximately 530-basis-point gap between the two metrics is composed of several recurring and non-recurring adjustments. Stock-based compensation charged to cost of goods sold — a function of equity grants to manufacturing and process engineering personnel — accounts for one tranche. Purchase accounting amortization of acquired intangibles represents the larger structural component: onsemi's 2016 acquisition of Fairchild Semiconductor, a $2.4 billion transaction, left a substantial intangible asset base on the balance sheet that continued to amortize through cost of goods sold years after close, as did the $415 million GTAT acquisition completed in November 2021. These amortization charges will diminish over time as the intangible assets reach full amortization, mechanically narrowing the GAAP-to-non-GAAP divergence without any operational improvement required. Restructuring charges recorded through fiscal 2025 — associated with ongoing footprint rationalization and the earlier write-off of the Quantenna communications division — further widened the divergence in reported periods.

The non-GAAP operating margin of 18.6% in fiscal 2025 against a GAAP operating margin of 1.4% tells the same story at the operating level, amplified by above-the-line impairment charges. For comparative and trend purposes, the non-GAAP series is the operative performance signal, and at 18.6% operating margin on a revenue base 27% below peak, the business demonstrated a degree of cost-base resilience the commodity model of 2019 could not have generated.

## Free Cash Flow: The Metric That Redefined the Investment Case

onsemi generated [$1,759.8 million in operating cash flow](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001097864/000109786426000006/on-20251231.htm) during fiscal 2025. Capital expenditure of $341.2 million — derived as the residual — produced [free cash flow of $1,418.6 million](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0), representing a 24.0% free cash flow margin on $5,995 million in revenue. That figure demands context. Companies operating vertically integrated manufacturing models — as onsemi does for SiC, from crystal growth through device fabrication — typically report lower free cash flow margins than fabless peers precisely because the owned-fab model demands sustained capital expenditure to maintain process competitiveness and expand capacity. onsemi's 24% free cash flow margin, achieved at cyclical trough revenue, reflected the completion of the major phase of SiC capital investment centered on the East Fishkill, New York fabrication facility. Management had guided toward declining CapEx intensity as the East Fishkill ramp approached full utilization; the fiscal 2025 CapEx figure confirmed that trajectory, representing a fraction of the capital intensity that characterized the 2022–2023 greenfield investment phase. As revenue recovers toward the $6.3–$6.5 billion forward run-rate and CapEx remains at maintenance-and-efficiency levels rather than greenfield-expansion levels, free cash flow generation is structurally positioned to expand in absolute terms even before any margin improvement is credited.

## Balance Sheet: Conservative Leverage and Maturity Management

As of December 31, 2025, [onsemi's balance sheet showed $2,147.6 million in cash and cash equivalents alongside $400.0 million in short-term investments](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001097864/000109786426000006/on-20251231.htm), for total liquid assets of $2,547.6 million. Long-term debt stood at $2,980.5 million, composed primarily of convertible notes at staggered maturities and drawn revolving credit. At year-end, management repaid $375 million outstanding on the revolving credit facility, restoring approximately $1.5 billion of revolving credit availability.

Net leverage — total debt minus total liquid assets — was approximately $433 million as of year-end 2025. Against trailing non-GAAP EBITDA that substantially exceeded $1.5 billion, net leverage represented well below 0.3 times — a conservative capital structure relative to the semiconductor peer group and a marked contrast to the leveraged-buyout structure the company inherited from the 1999 Motorola spinout.

| Metric | Value (Dec 31, 2025) |
|---|---|
| Cash & equivalents | $2,147.6M |
| Short-term investments | $400.0M |
| Total liquidity | $2,547.6M |
| Long-term debt | $2,980.5M |
| Net debt | ~$433M |
| Revolver availability | ~$1,500M |
| Net leverage (vs. EBITDA) | <0.3x |

The contrast with Wolfspeed, onsemi's most direct SiC competitor, was instructive: Wolfspeed carried net debt well in excess of 10 times EBITDA through 2025 and faced sustained questions about its ability to fund the capital programs necessary to remain competitive. OEM procurement teams evaluating long-term SiC supply agreements weigh supplier financial health alongside technical qualification — a dynamic that allowed onsemi to bid from a position of visible balance sheet durability that Wolfspeed could not match. The convertible note structure embedded in the debt stack introduces maturity concentration risk that bears monitoring as principal payment dates approach. No single maturity appeared to present an imminent liquidity concern given the revolver availability and free cash flow generation profile, but refinancing decisions through 2027–2028 will need to be executed against interest rate conditions and stock price levels that may differ materially from original issuance terms.

## Recovery Signals and the Q2 2026 Guidance Envelope

The sequential margin recovery from Q2 2025 through Q1 2026 constituted the most concrete evidence that the inventory correction had largely cleared. Non-GAAP gross margin moved from approximately 37.6% at the trough to [38.2% in Q4 2025](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0) and then [38.5% in Q1 2026](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-first-quarter-2026-gs4gw3jyioon) — three consecutive quarters of improvement even as absolute revenue remained compressed relative to prior-cycle levels. The directional signal was reinforced by AI data-center revenue growing more than 30% sequentially in Q1 2026, a product mix tailwind that management expected to compound through the year as hyperscaler and ODM customers continued to build out GPU cluster infrastructure using EliteSiC MOSFETs and JFETs for 48V rack power conversion.

The Q2 2026 guidance of $1,540 million to $1,640 million in revenue with non-GAAP gross margin of 37.4% to 39.4% and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.65 to $0.77 embedded meaningful uncertainty at both ends of the range. The lower bound accommodated product mix variation that could temporarily compress margin; the upper bound reflected continued SiC and AI datacenter contribution growth. A straight annualization of the midpoint implies approximately $6.36 billion in revenue — and if management's full-year AI data-center guidance above $500 million is met, the implied back-half H2 2026 acceleration toward $600 million or more in that segment alone argues for gross margin progression above the mid-year trough, driving the full-year non-GAAP EPS toward the $2.60–$2.80 range that sell-side consensus had established.

## The Buyback Arithmetic and Share Count Reduction

The [$6 billion share repurchase authorization announced in November 2025](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0), to be executed over three years, represented one of the more aggressive capital return commitments in the semiconductor peer group measured as a percentage of market capitalization — approximately 12% of the then-prevailing market cap. In fiscal 2025 alone, the company returned $1.4 billion, equivalent to 100% of free cash flow generated during the year, entirely through share repurchases, materially reducing the diluted share count.

The per-share earnings accretion from sustained buybacks is mechanically straightforward. At approximately 375–380 million diluted shares outstanding, a $2 billion annual repurchase program — the implied pace of the $6 billion three-year authorization — at blended average prices below the intrinsic value implied by the company's free cash flow yield would retire approximately 15 to 20 million shares annually, or 4% to 5% of the diluted count per year. Holding net income flat, that reduction produces commensurate annualized accretion to diluted EPS without any requirement for revenue or margin growth. Over the full authorization period, if the $6 billion is fully deployed, the cumulative share count reduction could approach 15% to 20%, transforming modest absolute net income growth into substantially higher per-share earnings progression. GAAP diluted EPS of $0.29 in fiscal 2025 — depressed by impairment and restructuring charges that investors attributed to accounting rather than operations — offered little informational content; non-GAAP diluted EPS of $2.35 for the same period was the operative figure, and the buyback program was engineered to make that figure compound faster than the underlying business itself.

chapters.title: What the Market Is Pricing In: Multiple Analysis, Peer Comparisons, and Scenario Valuations
chapters.body:
## A Stock Re-Rated, Then Re-Questioned

By late May 2026, ON Semiconductor's shares had staged one of the more striking recoveries in the analog and power semiconductor space. Trading at approximately $131–$135 per share, onsemi carried a market capitalisation of roughly $49–$51 billion and an enterprise value of approximately $50–$53 billion once net debt of $433 million was added back. The trailing twelve-month non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.35 — the figure the company reported for full-year 2025 against a backdrop of the deepest revenue trough since Hassane El-Khoury took the helm — put the trailing price-to-earnings multiple at a seemingly rich 56x. That figure, however, was largely an artefact of cyclical compression rather than structural deterioration: sell-side consensus for FY2026 non-GAAP EPS of approximately $2.60–$2.80 collapsed the forward multiple to 22–23x, a reading the market appeared to treat as the more meaningful anchor. Forward EV/EBITDA of roughly 15–17x completed the picture of a stock that had re-rated meaningfully from its early-2026 lows but had not fully reclaimed the premium assigned at the height of the EV-semiconductor frenzy.

The approximately 90% year-to-date rally that carried onsemi to that May 2026 price level was itself a compound story: automotive inventory digestion at tier-one suppliers had shown credible signs of clearing, Q1 2026 AI data-centre revenue had grown more than 30% sequentially, and management's guidance of full-year 2026 AI data-centre revenue above $500 million had given investors a second growth vector to price alongside the SiC automotive recovery. [onsemi Q1 2026 earnings release](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-first-quarter-2026-gs4gw3jyioon). The stock, in other words, arrived at its May 2026 valuation carrying two partially-corroborated theses rather than one, which changed the risk calculus relative to the pure-play EV story that had dominated the 2021–2022 bull run.

## Where onsemi Sits Among Its Peers

A cross-section of the power and automotive semiconductor peer group as of late May 2026 illustrates both the relative valuation and the competitive framing:

| Company | Approx. Market Cap (USD) | Forward P/E | EV/EBITDA (Fwd) | EV/Sales (Fwd) | P/B | Peer Category |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **onsemi (ON)** | ~$50B | ~22–23x | ~15–17x | ~2.8x | ~4.5x | SiC & automotive |
| STMicroelectronics (STM) | ~$25B | ~18–20x | ~10–12x | ~2.0x | ~2.8x | SiC direct competitor; automotive |
| Infineon Technologies (IFX) | ~$40B | ~20–22x | ~12–14x | ~2.4x | ~3.0x | SiC direct competitor; automotive |
| NXP Semiconductors (NXPI) | ~$55B | ~18–20x | ~13–15x | ~3.2x | ~6.0x | Automotive semiconductor peer |
| Texas Instruments (TXN) | ~$185B | ~33–36x | ~22–24x | ~10.5x | ~35x | Analog/power peer; mature FCF model |
| Wolfspeed (WOLF) | ~$3B | NM (loss) | NM | ~2.0x | ~1.2x | SiC direct competitor; distressed |

The table positions onsemi as a moderate-premium name within the automotive semiconductor cohort. Its 22–23x forward P/E exceeded STMicro's 18–20x and roughly tracked Infineon's 20–22x, reflecting the market's view that onsemi's SiC design-win depth and AI data-centre optionality warranted a slight uplift over European peers still digesting their own automotive inventory cycles. The discount to Texas Instruments was sharp but structurally justified: TI's 33–36x multiple reflected the near-consensus view that TI's analogue franchise generated durable, capital-light free cash flow across cycles in a way that onsemi's vertically integrated, EV-exposed SiC model could not yet match. Wolfspeed's near-distressed multiple served as a cautionary data point — a pure-play SiC competitor burdened by debt taken on to fund fab construction that demand had not yet absorbed, representing the downside scenario onsemi's management explicitly sought to avoid by completing its own CapEx cycle while the balance sheet remained conservative.

## The Historical Multiple Corridor

To calibrate the current 22–23x reading, it is instructive to trace onsemi's multiple through the EV semiconductor cycle. In 2019 — before El-Khoury's appointment and at the company's pre-transformation revenue base of roughly $5.5 billion — onsemi traded at a modest 10–14x forward non-GAAP earnings, consistent with a legacy mixed-signal house whose automotive exposure was broad but undifferentiated.

The transformation thesis, once articulated and initially validated through design-win announcements, catalysed a pronounced re-rating. By late 2021 and into 2022, as EV adoption curves looked nearly exponential and SiC appeared supply-constrained for years, onsemi's forward P/E expanded toward 35–40x and at moments touched higher. The stock briefly traded above $90 in late 2021 — a level that implied embedded optimism that has been only partially vindicated by subsequent SiC revenue outcomes. The multiple then compressed sharply through 2023–2024 as automotive production plateaued, OEM EV build plans were revised downward, and Chinese SiC suppliers accelerated their cost-down trajectories. At trough, the forward multiple dipped into the 14–16x range, levels last associated with the pre-transformation commodity model — a market signal that investor confidence in the SiC premium had materially eroded.

The May 2026 reading of 22–23x forward P/E therefore sits near the midpoint of a rough five-year range of approximately 14x to 40x, with the upper bound an artefact of peak EV exuberance and the lower bound a moment of maximum pessimism about automotive demand recovery. Measured against the cycle-adjusted midpoint of that corridor — call it 20–24x — the stock appeared approximately fairly valued at the frozen snapshot date, embedding a moderate recovery expectation without returning to the euphoria that preceded it.

## Scenario Framework: Three Paths from the 2025 Trough

**Bull case.** The thesis resolves as management guided: SiC revenue recovers to $2.5 billion or above by FY2027 as North American and European EV OEM production volumes ramp under model refreshes and new platform launches, and AI data-centre revenue compounds to $1 billion or more annually as Intel and Nvidia ecosystem customers consume onsemi's image sensor and power management solutions at scale. Operating leverage on a largely fixed SiC manufacturing base drives non-GAAP EPS toward $4.00 by FY2028. At a 25–28x forward earnings multiple — the premium a semiconductor investor would assign to a business demonstrating SiC gross margins converging toward 50% — the implied equity value reaches $100–$112 per share on FY2028 earnings, representing meaningful upside even from the elevated May 2026 price. The single variable that makes this case: SiC revenue re-acceleration, not merely stabilisation, in FY2026 and FY2027.

**Base case.** SiC revenue stabilises in the $1.8–$2.0 billion range by FY2026–FY2027, growing but not reclaiming the peak narrative. AI data-centre revenue reaches $600–$700 million in FY2027, a meaningful contributor but insufficient to offset a modest SiC pricing headwind from Chinese competitors. Non-GAAP EPS converges to $2.80–$3.20 by FY2027. At a 20–22x forward multiple — consistent with a well-managed automotive semiconductor company without a transformational premium — implied equity value lands in the $56–$70 per share range. The key variable: whether SiC margins hold at current levels or compress by 200–400 basis points as the competitive field widens.

**Bear case.** EV demand disappoints structurally — not cyclically — as hybrid powertrains absorb a larger share of the transition and full-BEV volumes undershoot OEM production plans through 2027. Chinese SiC module suppliers, led by BYD and domestic tier-ones, take meaningful share from onsemi in the cost-sensitive mid-power segment. Image sensor market share, currently anchored by long-cycle ADAS design wins, faces erosion from Sony's automotive expansion. AI data-centre adoption of onsemi products proves slower to scale than guided. EPS stalls below $2.50. At 15–18x — the commodity-semiconductor multiple assigned before the El-Khoury transformation — implied equity value falls to $37–$45 per share. The triggering variable: structural rather than cyclical SiC demand disappointment, which would challenge the core premise that El-Khoury permanently raised the company's revenue floor.

## DCF Sensitivity: The FCF Margin Question

The free cash flow margin of 24.0% that onsemi achieved in FY2025 — on revenue that was itself cyclically depressed — stands as perhaps the most important financial disclosure of the year. Whether it is sustainable or a temporary artefact of a completed CapEx cycle is the central DCF variable. The company had substantially finished its multi-year SiC fabrication investment by end-FY2025; maintenance CapEx and incremental capacity additions should require less capital intensity than the greenfield phase. But if revenue recovers toward $7–8 billion and management pursues second-generation SiC capacity for post-2028 design wins, FCF margin could normalise lower.

The following sensitivity table estimates net present value per share across revenue growth and FCF margin assumptions (using a 10% discount rate, 15-year horizon, 15x terminal EBITDA multiple):

| Long-Term Revenue CAGR | FCF Margin 20% | FCF Margin 22% | FCF Margin 24% |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3%** | ~$42 | ~$50 | ~$58 |
| **5%** | ~$60 | ~$72 | ~$84 |
| **7%** | ~$85 | ~$101 | ~$118 |

At the frozen snapshot price of approximately $133, the market's implied assumption sits somewhere in the 5–7% long-term revenue growth, 22–24% FCF margin quadrant — consistent with the base-to-bull transition zone but requiring sustained execution on both the SiC recovery and the AI data-centre ramp. The 3% growth / 20% margin cell, at roughly $42 per share, effectively prices in the bear case; only at 7% growth and 24% FCF margin does the DCF approach the current market price, confirming that the stock at May 2026 levels was not cheap on intrinsic-value terms.

## What the Market Is Actually Saying

The approximately 22–23x forward earnings multiple that onsemi carried at the frozen snapshot date encoded a specific and identifiable market judgement: moderate confidence in the SiC recovery, nascent but growing confidence in the AI data-centre ramp, and a material hedge against the bear scenario of Chinese competition and EV demand disappointment. It was a materially different signal than the 35–40x the stock commanded at the 2021–2022 peak, when investors assigned near-certainty to the SiC supply supercycle and treated onsemi as the infrastructure bottleneck for the EV transition. That peak multiple implicitly valued onsemi as a growth compounder; the May 2026 multiple valued it as a well-managed industrial technology company with credible but unproven recovery vectors.

The contrast matters beyond the arithmetic. Investor risk appetite for EV semiconductor stories had demonstrably repriced between 2022 and 2026 — a repricing that onsemi's two-vector strategy, adding AI data-centre revenue to SiC automotive, was explicitly designed to address. Whether the market would ultimately reward that strategic addition with a sustained premium above 22–23x depended on one thing above all others: whether SiC revenue re-acceleration arrived on the schedule that design-win disclosures implied, or whether the curve bent further right under competitive and demand pressure.

chapters.title: The Quarterly Narrative: From SiC Supercycle to Inventory Correction to AI Inflection
chapters.body:
## The Supercycle Quarter and Its Aftermath

By the time onsemi reported its third-quarter 2023 results, Hassane El-Khoury had transformed a Motorola commodity spinout into what the market was briefly treating as the purest play on the electrification supercycle. With the company running at an annualised revenue pace approaching the $8.25 billion it would record for the full year, management language on earnings calls had shifted from guarded optimism to frank confidence. El-Khoury and his team characterised the SiC design-win pipeline as multi-year and largely locked, pointing to the Vitesco $1.9 billion supply agreement and the BMW traction-inverter partnership as evidence that European OEM platforms were now permanently wired to EliteSiC. The stock had appreciated roughly five-fold from El-Khoury's December 2020 arrival, and sell-side analysts competed to raise price targets.

What came next was one of the more instructive inventory cycles in the recent history of automotive semiconductors.

## The Correction Deepens: 2024

Through fiscal 2024, revenue declined to $7,082.3 million from the $8,252.4 million recorded in 2023 — a 14.2 per cent contraction that onsemi initially characterised as a temporary digestion of excess channel inventory at tier-1 automotive suppliers. El-Khoury acknowledged in successive quarterly calls that the correction was proving longer than the company had initially projected. Tier-1s such as Continental, Vitesco, and BorgWarner had built forward inventory in 2022 and early 2023 in anticipation of continued supply tightness; when EV production schedules at European OEMs began to slip against aggressive electrification targets, those channel buffers became a ceiling on fresh onsemi orders.

Non-GAAP gross margins through 2024 held roughly in the mid-to-high 38 per cent range on a quarterly basis, providing some cushion against the revenue decline and lending credibility to management's thesis that the underlying product mix — premium SiC MOSFETs, automotive image sensors, and application-specific analog — was structurally superior to the commodity model it had replaced. The stock, however, reflected investor doubt. Shares that had touched highs above $115 in 2023 retreated through the year as the duration of the correction exceeded original estimates.

## Trough and Turning Point: The 2025 Quarters

Fiscal 2025 produced the deepest revenue decline of the El-Khoury era. Full-year revenue of $5,995.4 million represented a further 15.3 per cent decline from 2024, driven by the continued automotive inventory purge and a temporary moderation in SiC demand as EV OEMs — particularly Chinese NEV producers — recalibrated production build plans against softer-than-expected consumer demand. Non-GAAP gross margin compressed to a trough near 37.6 per cent in the second quarter of 2025, a level that prompted pointed analyst questions about the durability of the restructured margin profile.

The second quarter nonetheless contained an early signal of the narrative that would define the back half of the year. China revenue grew 23 per cent sequentially, driven by new EV model ramps at BYD-adjacent supply chains and local tier-1 inverter suppliers. El-Khoury described the Chinese NEV business as a structural position rather than a tactical opportunity, noting that local OEM SiC content-per-vehicle was rising rapidly as Chinese automakers converged on 800-volt architectures.

Third-quarter 2025 — revenue of $1,550.9 million, non-GAAP gross margin 38.0 per cent, non-GAAP operating margin 19.2 per cent — marked a clear qualitative shift in management's earnings-call language. El-Khoury stated that the company was seeing

> "continued signs of stabilisation in our core automotive and industrial markets, alongside positive growth in AI, which is increasingly becoming a meaningful contributor."

The phrase "stabilisation" carried weight: it was the first time management had applied it to both automotive and industrial simultaneously rather than qualifying each with caveats about specific customers or geographies. Analysts noted the AI data-centre reference as a new construction — earlier calls had mentioned power supply design wins without connecting them explicitly to the AI infrastructure buildout. Non-GAAP operating margin of 19.2 per cent, while below the 2022–2023 peak levels, confirmed that the restructured cost base was holding through the revenue trough. The stock responded positively to the Q3 release, recovering ground lost earlier in the year.

## The FY2025 Full-Year Release: Capital Return as Conviction Signal

On 9 February 2026 onsemi reported fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 results. [Q4 revenue of $1,530.1 million](https://investor.onsemi.com/news-releases/news-release-details/onsemi-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-results-0) closed a fiscal year in which the company had demonstrated something arguably more important than revenue growth: free cash flow discipline at the trough. Record free cash flow of $1,418.6 million — a 24.0 per cent FCF margin on $5,995.4 million in revenue — was the headline number, and management returned the entirety of it to shareholders through repurchases, a statement of capital-allocation conviction that received prominent placement in the press release.

Chief Financial Officer Thad Trent offered the full-year framing directly:

> "With our major investment cycle behind us and new technologies ramping, we continue to strengthen our financial foundation."

The sentence was carefully constructed. "Major investment cycle behind us" signalled that the multi-year SiC wafer-fab capital programme — centring on the East Fishkill 200mm facility and the Hudson, New Hampshire GTAT crystal-growth operations — had reached a phase of harvest rather than construction. "New technologies ramping" pointed forward to both the AI data-centre SiC opportunity and the Treo platform's early design-win pipeline. On a GAAP basis, results were materially depressed: full-year GAAP gross margin of 33.1 per cent versus non-GAAP 38.4 per cent, GAAP operating margin of 1.4 per cent versus non-GAAP 18.6 per cent, and GAAP diluted EPS of $0.29 versus non-GAAP $2.35, the divergence driven primarily by restructuring charges, impairment write-downs, and purchase-accounting amortisation on the Fairchild and GTAT acquisitions.

Management guided first-quarter 2026 revenue of $1,435–$1,535 million and held the tone of cautious recovery — automotive stabilisation intact, AI growing, industrial still soft.

## Q1 2026: The AI Inflection Becomes Quantifiable

The first-quarter 2026 earnings release, published in early May 2026, provided the first quarter in which the AI data-centre narrative became numerically concrete. Revenue of $1,513 million beat the guidance midpoint by approximately $28 million. Non-GAAP gross margin expanded for the third consecutive quarter to 38.5 per cent, continuing a step-by-step recovery from the 2025 trough. The standout data point was AI data-centre revenue growing more than 30 per cent sequentially.

Management declared that AI data-centre revenue was on track to exceed $500 million for the full year 2026, implying approximately 100 per cent year-over-year growth from the 2025 base. The combination of EliteSiC MOSFETs and the Qorvo-acquired JFET topology — better suited to the high-frequency switching requirements of 48-volt rack power distribution units in GPU clusters — had positioned onsemi as a credible supplier to hyperscaler and ODM customers building AI server infrastructure. El-Khoury described the data-centre opportunity as a natural extension of the SiC power platform rather than a pivot.

For the second quarter of 2026, management guided revenue of $1,540–$1,640 million with non-GAAP EPS of $0.65–$0.77. The guidance midpoint of $1,590 million implied an annual run-rate approaching $6.3 billion, a pace meaningfully ahead of the 2025 trough and consistent with sell-side models projecting a two-year recovery arc back toward 2023 revenue levels.

| Metric | Q2 2025 (trough) | Q3 2025 | Q4 2025 | Q1 2026 | Q2 2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | ~$1,484M | $1,550.9M | $1,530.1M | $1,513M | $1,540–$1,640M |
| Non-GAAP Gross Margin | ~37.6% | 38.0% | ~38.2% | 38.5% | Expanding |
| Non-GAAP Operating Margin | — | 19.2% | — | — | — |

## The Questions Analysts Were Still Asking

Even as the sequential recovery hardened into a trend, three lines of investor scepticism persisted through the Q1 2026 earnings call and dominated the analyst question period.

The first centred on SiC revenue durability. Analysts pressed El-Khoury on whether the recovery in automotive SiC demand was broad-based or concentrated in Chinese NEV ramps that could prove transient. Domestic Chinese SiC producers — smaller but growing — were beginning to compete on price with tier-1 Chinese inverter suppliers, compressing average selling prices at the margin. The question was whether onsemi's European and North American design wins provided sufficient volume backstop if Chinese OEM exposure proved volatile.

The second line of questioning targeted AI data-centre revenue quality. Hyperscaler capex cycles are notoriously lumpy, and analysts sought reassurance that the 30 per cent sequential growth in Q1 was not a build-ahead of a single large programme. Management's response — that revenue was diversified across multiple hyperscaler and ODM customers and that the JFET topology provided a differentiated entry point unavailable to pure MOSFET competitors — was received with measured confidence rather than full conviction.

The third question was the most structurally important: when would non-GAAP gross margin return to the 45–47 per cent levels that onsemi had demonstrated at the 2022–2023 revenue peak? At 38.5 per cent in Q1 2026, margins remained roughly 700–800 basis points below the prior peaks, and management had not provided a specific timeline for recovery. The answer — that margin expansion would track revenue scale and the gradual improvement in SiC and Treo product mix — was accurate but left analysts without a firm commitment date, sustaining the discount at which ON shares traded relative to analog-semiconductor peers with more stable margin histories.

chapters.title: The Cypress Alumni Playbook: El-Khoury, Trent, and the Board That Governs the Transformation
chapters.body:
## The Cypress Alumni Arrive

When Hassane El-Khoury walked into onsemi's Scottsdale headquarters in December 2020, he recognized the company immediately — not from the product catalogues or the analyst reports, but from the structural profile. Here was a semiconductor business with genuine manufacturing depth, a sprawling customer base, and a balance sheet still carrying the weight of acquisitions made in the name of breadth rather than focus. Here was a business selling components into dozens of end-markets, measuring success in units shipped rather than platform commitments secured, and reporting gross margins that compelled nobody to lean forward in their seat. He had been here before. He had fixed one version of this before.

El-Khoury had spent the previous four years as President and CEO of Cypress Semiconductor, where he had executed a textbook repositioning — shrinking the product catalogue, concentrating engineering investment on automotive-grade microcontrollers and programmable system-on-chip products, and ultimately making Cypress attractive enough to Infineon Technologies that the German giant paid $9.5 billion for it in April 2020. The sale closed. The work was done. And then, eight months later, he was standing in front of a company that was, in some respects, a larger, rougher version of the same problem.

onsemi in late 2020 was not without assets. The 2016 acquisition of Fairchild Semiconductor had delivered wafer fabrication capacity, an established power discrete portfolio, and a meaningful automotive customer base. The 2011 acquisition of Sanyo Semiconductor had added Japanese manufacturing heritage. But the aggregate result was a company generating approximately $5.5 billion in annual revenue across commodity discretes, standard-logic ICs, image sensors, and Wi-Fi chipsets, with gross margins that had barely crossed 40% at the cycle peak and a strategic narrative fragmented across more end-markets than any investor could reasonably track. The Motorola spinout of 1999 — founded as a leveraged buyout of commodity jellybean components — had never fully shed its DNA.

## Hassane El-Khoury: The Engineer Who Learned to Allocate

El-Khoury, born in 1979, holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Lawrence Technological University, earned in 2001, and a Master of Science in Engineering Management from Oakland University, completed in 2006 — the latter credential reflecting an early and deliberate investment in the business architecture of engineering, not merely its technical execution. His career began at Continental Automotive Systems, where he worked as a senior design engineer, accumulating the domain knowledge of automotive electronics at the supplier level — an experience that would prove foundational. He understood how tier-1 suppliers specified components, how qualification cycles worked, and what a multi-year design commitment actually meant in practice before he had ever managed a business unit.

He joined Cypress Semiconductor in 2007 and spent the next nine years progressing through applications engineering, business development, and general management roles. By 2016 he was CEO, having been handed a company whose legacy NOR flash and SRAM businesses were facing structural decline from NAND substitution and mobile DRAM consolidation. The playbook he wrote at Cypress — exit commodity lines, concentrate on differentiated platforms, build long-cycle customer relationships in automotive and industrial, and communicate a simpler, more investable story to the market — became the template he carried to Scottsdale.

His language at onsemi has consistently reflected that prior experience. In investor settings, El-Khoury has distinguished sharply between "design wins" and "design-ins" — the former representing a contracted, multi-year platform commitment from a strategic customer, the latter a softer expression of interest that carries no revenue certainty. The distinction is not semantic; it is a cultural instruction to the commercial organisation. He came to onsemi with a network already cultivated across European and American automotive procurement, and with a conviction that the SiC transition in EV powertrains represented the right decade-long platform on which to stake the company's identity.

## Thad Trent: The CFO Who Counts Free Cash Flow First

Thad Trent joined onsemi as Chief Financial Officer in February 2021, approximately seven weeks after El-Khoury's arrival — a sequencing that speaks to the deliberateness of the pairing. The two men had worked together at Cypress for years. Trent first joined Cypress in 2005 and served as CFO from June 2014 through the Infineon close. At onsemi, he inherited a capital structure that included substantial acquisition-related debt and a share count that had grown through decades of equity-based compensation without the discipline of countervailing buybacks.

Trent's capital allocation philosophy, as demonstrated at both companies, prioritises free cash flow margin as the primary measure of business health, treats share repurchases as the preferred return mechanism in the absence of compelling M&A, and is resistant to dilutive equity issuance. At onsemi, the evidence of that philosophy is visible in the financial record: the company returned 100% of its $1.42 billion in 2025 free cash flow through buybacks, and in November 2025 the board authorised a new $6 billion repurchase programme over three years — representing roughly 12% of market capitalisation at the time of announcement, and implying approximately four years of completion at the then-prevailing FCF generation rate of roughly $1.4 billion annually.

The $6 billion authorisation is not an idle number. At a company generating SiC-driven revenue growth, the buyback programme operates in productive tension with continued capital expenditure in crystal growth and wafer fabrication. Trent has consistently framed the tension as a feature rather than a contradiction: the vertical integration investment is capacity-building for a supply-constrained market, while the buyback commitment signals that management does not expect to consume all available cash in endless capacity additions. In December 2025, Trent was appointed to the board of directors of Lumentum Holdings — an external validation of his standing as a capital allocator in the photonics and semiconductor supply chain, and a recognition that extends beyond the onsemi shareholder base.

## The Board: Independent Chair, Automotive Credibility

The governance architecture that oversees El-Khoury and Trent is defined, in the first instance, by the separation of the Chair and CEO roles — a structural feature that onsemi adopted to provide independent oversight of the management team and that distinguishes its governance from peers where the CEO also chairs the board. Alan Campbell serves as independent Chair, a position that carries both a formal oversight function and the implicit mandate to speak for the board in its relationship with the executive team.

The board composition disclosed in the 2025 proxy statement filed with the SEC in April 2025 reflects the strategic agenda in its membership profile. Directors with automotive industry operating experience, capital markets backgrounds, and semiconductor technology expertise sit alongside Campbell, bringing sector-relevant judgment to committee deliberations on M&A, capital structure, and compensation design. Committee assignments across Audit, Compensation, and Nominating and Governance functions distribute oversight responsibility without concentrating it in any single director.

## Aligning Incentives with the Transformation

The compensation architecture disclosed in the 2025 proxy is perhaps the clearest structural signal of management's stated intentions. Executive compensation at onsemi is heavily weighted toward long-term equity awards, with performance conditions tied to two metrics: relative total shareholder return versus the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) and non-GAAP earnings per share growth. The TSR component anchors management's reward directly to the company's performance against its peer group of semiconductor companies — a design that discourages short-term revenue maximisation at the expense of margin quality. The non-GAAP EPS component rewards the absolute earnings progression that comes from the mix-shift toward higher-margin SiC and imaging revenue and away from commodity discretes.

The design is consequential. A management team compensated primarily on revenue would have rational incentives to preserve legacy product lines, accept margin-dilutive design wins to sustain volume, and resist the discomfort of a portfolio rationalisation that shrinks the top line before it expands the bottom line. The compensation structure at onsemi is explicitly designed to defeat that dynamic — to make the margin-accretive pivot financially rewarding for the executives executing it, rather than penalising them for short-term revenue softness.

## The Quantenna Chapter: A Governance Scar

The Quantenna acquisition — $1 billion paid in June 2019 for a Wi-Fi 6E chipset company under then-CEO Keith Jackson — stands as the most visible governance failure in the recent history of the board. The rationale at the time was diversification into connected-home and IoT connectivity; the outcome was a division that did not survive contact with El-Khoury's strategic priorities. After failing to attract a buyer in 2021, onsemi shut down the Quantenna operation in 2022 and wrote off the investment, redeploying the engineering resources and management attention toward SiC and imaging.

The accountability question is complicated by the partial continuity of board membership between the 2019 acquisition approval and the 2022 exit. Some directors who were present when Quantenna was acquired remained on the board when El-Khoury arrived and when the write-off was taken. The current board has not publicly relitigated the Quantenna decision in governance documents; the proxy record treats it as a prior-regime transaction. The practical lesson the episode reinforces — for investors and for management alike — is that large adjacency acquisitions outside the company's core domain expertise carry asymmetric risk, a lesson that appears well-internalised in the disciplined, bolt-on character of subsequent transactions: the $415 million GTAT crystal growth acquisition in 2021, the $118.8 million Qorvo SiC JFET purchase in January 2025, each small relative to balance sheet capacity and each targeted at filling a specific gap in a defined supply chain.

## A Simpler Investor Story
