The investor relations posture under El-Khoury represents a deliberate departure from the fragmented multi-market messaging that characterised the prior era, when onsemi described itself to investors across computing, consumer, automotive, industrial, medical, and communications segments simultaneously — a taxonomy that accurately described where revenue came from but obscured what the company was actually trying to become.

The current narrative has been compressed to three end-markets — automotive, industrial, and cloud/AI data-centre — and three product pillars: EliteSiC power, intelligent image sensing, and the Treo analog platform. Capital allocation is described in terms of free cash flow generation and return, not in terms of revenue targets. Long-term supply agreements with named customers — Vitesco's $1.9 billion, ten-year commitment; the BMW and Volkswagen EV platform relationships — are cited as evidence of revenue durability rather than aspirational pipeline. It is a story designed to be held in the mind of a single portfolio manager reading a quarterly earnings transcript, and its discipline reflects the experience of two executives who have made this argument to institutional investors before and know which parts of it tend to get lost in translation.

chapters.title: Design Wins and Long-Term Agreements: onsemi's Customer Architecture Across Automotive, Industrial, and AI
chapters.body:
## From Catalog Sales to Platform Commitments

The most consequential structural change in onsemi's commercial model under Hassane El-Khoury was not a product launch or an acquisition — it was a fundamental reimagining of how the company sold. Before the 2020 transformation, onsemi operated largely as a transactional supplier: catalog components priced competitively, ordered at spot or short-cycle terms, with no contractual obligation binding customer volumes to onsemi's fabs. That model rewarded breadth over depth and left revenue exposed to every inventory swing in the automotive and industrial supply chain.

El-Khoury replaced that model with a design-win platform architecture underpinned by long-term supply agreements, or LTSAs. Under this structure, onsemi engages automotive customers — typically tier-1 systems integrators rather than OEMs directly — at the earliest stage of a new vehicle program, embedding its silicon carbide MOSFETs or image sensors into the subsystem reference design before the OEM specifications are frozen. Once the design win is secured, both parties negotiate an LTSA that specifies volume commitments, pricing mechanisms, and delivery schedules across the life of the vehicle model, typically three to five years of production. Pricing in these agreements is usually fixed or modestly indexed to input costs, insulating both parties from spot market volatility and providing onsemi with demand visibility stretching twelve to thirty-six months forward. OEM platform selection drives purchasing decisions from the tier-1 down the supply chain — when BMW or Volkswagen selects onsemi SiC for a traction inverter, the tier-1 assembling that inverter becomes a captive customer for the duration of that platform cycle.

## The Tier-1 Automotive Cluster

The clearest illustration of this model at scale is Vitesco Technologies. Spun off from Continental in 2021 as an independent electrification-focused powertrain supplier, Vitesco disclosed a $1.9 billion, ten-year SiC supply agreement with onsemi — the largest single customer contract publicly disclosed by the company. At approximately $190 million per year against onsemi's fiscal 2025 revenue base of $5,995.4 million, Vitesco represents roughly 3.2% of annual revenue: meaningful but not dominant. The product at the heart of the agreement is the EliteSiC 1200V MOSFET, integrated into Vitesco's traction inverter modules for 400V and 800V EV drivetrain architectures. Vitesco supplies these inverters to OEM customers across Europe and Asia, making the agreement a leveraged claim on multiple vehicle platforms simultaneously.

Continental — still a top-tier onsemi customer even after the Vitesco separation — continued to source SiC power modules and CMOS image sensors across its ADAS and electrification product lines. BorgWarner, which accelerated its electrification build-out through the Delphi Technologies and Wolfspeed inverter acquisitions, similarly draws on EliteSiC content in its eMotor and inverter systems. Bosch, the world's largest automotive supplier, was among the early tier-1 adopters of onsemi's automotive image sensors for its surround-view and front-facing ADAS camera modules. Aptiv — now focused on high-voltage electrical architecture and advanced safety systems — integrated onsemi components across its smart vehicle architecture platforms. None of these relationships carry individual disclosed contract values as large as the Vitesco agreement, but collectively the tier-1 cluster provides onsemi with embedded revenue across a majority of the world's EV production programs.

## BMW, Volkswagen, and the European Supply Chain Contest

Beyond the tier-1 layer, onsemi secured direct OEM-level strategic relationships with two of Europe's largest automakers. BMW Group disclosed a long-term supply agreement to integrate EliteSiC technology into its next-generation electric vehicle traction inverter architecture — a relationship that positioned onsemi's SiC modules inside one of the premium segment's highest-volume EV programs. Volkswagen Group announced a strategic SiC partnership with onsemi in January 2023, targeting traction module supply for its MEB and PPE electric platforms, which collectively underpin Volkswagen, Audi, Porsche, and ŠKODA EVs.

The strategic importance of these European OEM relationships extends beyond their immediate revenue contribution. STMicroelectronics — with approximately 35% global SiC MOSFET market share and deep Franco-Italian OEM relationships — had historically dominated European automotive SiC supply. Infineon Technologies, headquartered in Munich, carries native German relationships with BMW, Volkswagen, and Mercedes-Benz that give it structural proximity advantages in specification cycles. Against these incumbents, onsemi's pitch rested on supply chain resilience: a vertically integrated SiC manufacturing footprint anchored in the United States, with wafer-slicing and epitaxy capabilities that are not dependent on the same Asian substrate suppliers that constrain STMicroelectronics and Infineon at periods of peak demand. European OEM procurement teams — acutely sensitive to supply concentration risk after the 2021–2022 chip shortage — treated geographic supply diversification as a genuine specification criterion, not merely a procurement checkbox. onsemi's internal SiC crystal growth capability, acquired through the November 2021 GTAT transaction for $415 million, was a direct response to this dynamic.

## China: Fastest Growth, Deepest Risk

China's new-energy vehicle market produced the fastest sequential revenue growth in onsemi's automotive book. Revenue from China grew 23% sequentially in the second quarter of 2025, driven by new EV program ramps at Chinese NEV OEMs and the tier-1 inverter suppliers that serve them. onsemi's China customer base is structured primarily through supply-chain integrators — local tier-1s building inverters for SAIC, GAC, BYD-adjacent programs, and Zeekr — rather than through direct OEM relationships, reflecting the dominant role of domestic systems integrators in China's EV manufacturing ecosystem.

The geopolitical dimension of this exposure is non-trivial. Chinese domestic SiC producers — Sanan Optoelectronics, SICC (Sino Crystal Semiconductor), and TankeBlue Semiconductor — were advancing rapidly along the SiC substrate and device manufacturing curve as of early 2026, supported by government industrial policy, state-linked capital, and a captive domestic customer base that is increasingly receptive to local sourcing. The risk horizon for onsemi is not immediate displacement — Chinese domestic SiC MOSFETs remained behind onsemi's EliteSiC portfolio in device performance and reliability certification as of the frozen snapshot — but the 2026–2028 period presents a credible scenario in which Chinese OEM supply chains progressively substitute domestic SiC content, particularly at the lower-voltage 650V tier where performance differentiation is smaller. onsemi's response was to accelerate design-win depth within China, securing position in performance-sensitive 800V inverter programs where domestic alternatives remain less competitive.

## AI Data Centers: The Emerging Third Pillar

Outside automotive, onsemi's fastest-growing customer cluster as of 2026 was not named in any public disclosure. Hyperscaler infrastructure teams and ODMs building AI server rack infrastructure purchased EliteSiC MOSFETs and JFETs for 48V rack power distribution unit and power supply unit applications, where GPU cluster power density — driven by NVIDIA H100 and successor architectures drawing multiple kilowatts per server — required silicon carbide's superior switching efficiency at high voltage and high frequency. The Qorvo JFET technology acquired in January 2025 for $118.8 million directly addressed the AC-DC conversion stage of these PSUs, where JFET topology outperforms conventional MOSFETs at the switching frequencies required by modern high-density power rails.

Management provided unusually specific forward guidance on this segment. AI data-center revenue grew more than 30% sequentially in Q1 2026, and the company guided full-year FY2026 AI revenue above $500 million — implying approximately 100% year-over-year growth. El-Khoury characterized the data-center ramp as a structural shift rather than a pull-forward, pointing to the persistent gap between GPU rack power requirements and the efficiency ceiling of legacy silicon-based PSU designs as the fundamental driver.

## Customer Concentration and Revenue Policy

onsemi's 10-K customer concentration disclosures confirmed that no single customer represented 10% or more of total revenue in fiscal 2025, placing the company outside the SEC's mandatory named-customer disclosure threshold. The Vitesco LTSA, at an implied $190 million per year against $5,995.4 million in total fiscal 2025 revenue, illustrates the structure of that exposure: the largest single disclosed agreement represents approximately 3.2% of the annual revenue base — meaningful within a segment but not sufficient to create existential concentration risk. The tier-1 cluster in aggregate — Vitesco, Continental, BorgWarner, Bosch, Aptiv, and their OEM-linked programs — represents a far larger share of total automotive revenue, but because onsemi sells into these accounts across dozens of distinct product families and vehicle programs, the revenue is distributed across many invoice lines rather than concentrated in a single account.

| Customer / Cluster | Product Category | Disclosed Terms | Approx. Annual Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vitesco Technologies | EliteSiC 1200V MOSFET (traction inverter) | $1.9B, 10-year LTSA | ~$190M/year |
| BMW Group | EliteSiC traction inverter SiC | LTSA disclosed, terms undisclosed | Not disclosed |
| Volkswagen Group | SiC traction modules (MEB/PPE) | Strategic partnership, Jan 2023 | Not disclosed |
| Hyundai/Kia | SiC (E-GMP platform) | Design win disclosed | Not disclosed |
| China NEV tier-1s | EliteSiC MOSFETs | Transactional + design wins | Growing; +23% QoQ Q2 2025 |
| AI hyperscalers/ODMs | EliteSiC MOSFETs, JFETs (48V PSU) | Not individually disclosed | $500M+ FY2026 guided |

The architecture that emerges from this customer map is deliberate: deep platform embedding at the tier-1 layer, OEM-level strategic agreements that lock in specifications before design freeze, geographic diversification across European, Korean, and Chinese EV supply chains, and an AI data-center overlay that provides counter-cyclical exposure to a demand signal uncorrelated with automotive production schedules. The LTSAs provide the demand-side visibility that onsemi's vertically integrated SiC fabs require to plan crystal growth and wafer starts — binding the commercial architecture to the manufacturing architecture in a flywheel that commodity component sellers, with their transactional order books, cannot easily replicate.

chapters.title: The SiC Wars: onsemi's Position Against STMicroelectronics, Infineon, Wolfspeed, and Chinese Challengers
chapters.body:
## A Market With Three Fronts

By 2025, the silicon carbide power device market had crystallised into a hierarchy that onsemi's management tracked with the intensity of a military campaign. At the top sat STMicroelectronics, the Swiss-French conglomerate that controlled roughly 35% of global SiC revenue and had parlayed its early relationship with Tesla into the dominant position in automotive traction inverters. Behind it, onsemi held approximately 25% of the market, its EliteSiC MOSFET portfolio the principal weapon. Infineon Technologies sat third with roughly 15%, its CoolSiC line growing steadily through European OEM channels. Then came a second tier of pure-play specialists and, below them, a fast-moving Chinese cohort that threatened to reshape pricing dynamics in the world's largest EV market before the decade was out.

For Hassane El-Khoury, each front demanded a different response. Against STMicro and Infineon, the contest was for design wins at global OEMs, fought on technical differentiation and supply security. Against Wolfspeed, the dynamic had shifted from competition to opportunity as the former Cree pure-play entered financial crisis. And against the Chinese producers, the principal question was whether onsemi's vertical integration and premium product positioning could survive margin compression in a market that Beijing was determined to domesticate.

## STMicroelectronics: The Leader to Chase

STMicroelectronics earned its market leadership the hard way. Its early supply agreement with Tesla for Model 3 traction inverters established ST's SiC MOSFETs as the reference design for the generation of EV architectures that followed, creating installed-base momentum that smaller rivals spent years trying to disrupt. ST extended those relationships across Stellantis, BYD's domestic supply chain, and multiple European tier-1 inverter manufacturers, accumulating a customer roster that gave it manufacturing scale advantages and, with them, pricing leverage.

ST's structural advantage in substrates came from its 2019 acquisition of Norstel AB, a Swedish SiC wafer producer, which it paired with its own epitaxial deposition and device fabrication capabilities to build an integrated supply chain broadly analogous to onsemi's GTAT-anchored model. Where onsemi grew boules in Hudson, New Hampshire and sliced wafers for its East Fishkill fab, ST converted Norstel output through its Catania, Sicily operations — a geography that also drew EU semiconductor-sovereignty subsidies unavailable to onsemi's North American facilities.

The competitive battleground between the two companies concentrated on 650V and 1200V SiC MOSFETs for traction inverters and onboard chargers. At 650V, the fight was largely about switching speed and on-resistance at elevated junction temperatures — specs where onsemi's EliteSiC M3S generation made credible claims against ST's latest series. At 1200V, the contest shifted toward robustness in 800V EV architectures, a segment onsemi prioritised in its BMW and Volkswagen design wins. The two companies' automotive revenue compositions were similar enough that their financial trajectories through the 2024–2025 inventory correction became a natural mirror: both suffered top-line compression as EV build rates came in below projections, and both leaned on non-GAAP metrics to sustain investor confidence through the trough.

## Infineon: The European Platform Player

Infineon Technologies represented a different type of competitive threat — one whose SiC ambitions were embedded within a broader automotive semiconductor platform that included microcontrollers, radar front-ends, and safety logic. Its 2020 acquisition of Cypress Semiconductor, which El-Khoury himself had led as CEO before departing in the deal's wake, added body-domain controllers and automotive-grade memory to a suite that already included the AURIX family of safety microcontrollers running in nearly every European OEM's powertrain and chassis stack. This portfolio integration gave Infineon cross-selling leverage that a pure-power or pure-sensing specialist could not replicate at the system design table.

Infineon's CoolSiC MOSFET line was growing its share within Europe, where relationships with BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen Group had been cultivated over decades of IGBT and silicon-MOSFET supply. The structural advantage was geographic: European OEMs historically sourced power semiconductors from European and German-speaking suppliers, and Infineon's Villach, Austria fab — which anchored its SiC device manufacturing — was a few hours' drive from BMW's Munich engineering centres. onsemi's countermeasure lay in its disclosed long-term SiC agreements with both BMW and Volkswagen, which demonstrated that El-Khoury had penetrated Infineon's home-field advantage at the continent's two largest automotive groups. The durability of those wins in subsequent design cycles would be a key indicator of whether onsemi had genuinely displaced Infineon in European OEM preference or merely claimed a secondary supplier position.

## Wolfspeed: Distress as Opportunity

No development in the SiC competitive landscape carried more immediate strategic consequence for onsemi than Wolfspeed's descent into financial crisis. The Durham, North Carolina pure-play — which controlled a substantial share of global SiC wafer supply through its substrate business and had invested billions in the Mohawk Valley fab in Marcy, New York — entered 2025 burdened by debt it had accumulated to fund that expansion at precisely the moment automotive SiC demand growth slowed. Reports of restructuring talks circulated through 2024, and Wolfspeed's losses and balance sheet stress created what supply-chain professionals termed a credibility gap: OEM procurement teams that had considered sole-sourcing SiC from Wolfspeed began re-evaluating the risk of strategic dependency on a financially distressed supplier.

onsemi's management made no secret of its intent to benefit from that hesitation. El-Khoury described the environment as creating natural inbound interest from customers seeking supply assurance, and the company's track record of long-term agreements — the $1.9 billion, decade-long Vitesco commitment being the most public — became a marketing asset in conversations with Wolfspeed's nervous customers. The dynamic was not purely opportunistic: onsemi had also been a buyer of SiC substrates from Wolfspeed before the GTAT acquisition closed, so it understood intimately where Wolfspeed's wafer quality and lead times sat relative to alternatives. The open question heading into 2026 was whether the design-win reallocation that management described in earnings commentary would manifest as incremental revenue share in the 2027–2028 design cycle, when newly won programmes would begin production ramp.

## The Chinese Horizon

The third-tier threat operated on a different timeline but posed the most structural risk to long-term margin. SICC, Sanan Optoelectronics' SiC subsidiary, TankeBlue Semiconductor, and a cluster of state-backed producers had been scaling domestic SiC crystal growth and wafer production with subsidy support from Beijing's semiconductor self-sufficiency programmes. By 2025, Chinese SiC device makers were supplying a meaningful share of domestic NEV OEM demand — particularly in cost-sensitive mid-range platforms — at price points that Western incumbents acknowledged were below their own cost structures.

onsemi's exposure to this dynamic was double-edged. Its China revenue had grown 23% sequentially in Q2 2025 as domestic EV ramps accelerated, but that growth relied on Chinese customers choosing Western SiC for premium or export-destined models where performance standards and reliability certification remained differentiators. As domestic Chinese SiC producers improved their 1200V device reliability and pushed toward second-generation 150mm wafer technology, the certification gap would narrow. onsemi's vertical integration and accumulated automotive qualification data constituted a moat, but not an impregnable one.

## Image Sensors: Durable Leadership Under Pressure

onsemi's claim to the number-one position in automotive CMOS image sensors by revenue reflected years of design-win accumulation in surround-view cameras, front-facing ADAS stacks, and driver monitoring systems — a portfolio that Sony Semiconductor Solutions was actively challenging. Sony's IMX automotive series, developed through its automotive division, brought the imaging quality and low-light performance of Sony's dominant smartphone sensor heritage to the ADAS camera market, backed by an R&D budget that dwarfed onsemi's ISG division in absolute terms.

The competitive question was not whether Sony was a credible threat — it was — but whether the switching costs embedded in automotive sensor qualification cycles gave onsemi sufficient runway to maintain premium pricing through the current design-win generation. Camera module suppliers had typically qualified onsemi sensors into specific OEM programmes under multi-year contracts, meaning competitive displacement required winning the *next* programme rather than the current one. Samsung's automotive sensor ambitions and OmniVision's backing from Will Semiconductor added further pressure at the tier-2 level, but neither had yet demonstrated the automotive-grade reliability certification depth that onsemi and Sony maintained.

## Treo vs. the Analog Catalogue Giants

Against Texas Instruments, Microchip Technology, and Renesas Electronics, onsemi's Treo platform competed not on catalogue breadth — TI alone offered tens of thousands of analog SKUs — but on process node integration and thermal tolerance. Treo's 65nm BCD architecture, supporting 1–90V operation and junction temperatures to 175°C, was positioned as a single platform from which onsemi could derive automotive LED drivers, ultrasonic sensor AFEs, multi-phase controllers, and ADAS power management ICs without the customer engineering effort required to integrate components from multiple vendors' catalogues.

| Competitor | SiC Market Share (est.) | Key Automotive Strength | Primary Competitive Pressure on onsemi |
|---|---|---|---|
| STMicroelectronics | ~35% | Tesla, BYD, Stellantis incumbency | Pricing pressure, substrate integration |
| onsemi | ~25% | BMW, VW, Vitesco LTAs | Displacing ST at Tier-1s |
| Infineon | ~15% | European OEM platform breadth | CoolSiC ramp, AURIX cross-sell |
| Wolfspeed | ~8–10% | Wafer supply, pure-play | Financial distress, design-win risk |
| Chinese producers | ~10–12% | Domestic NEV cost position | Long-term margin compression |

Whether Treo's integration argument translated to measurable design-win share gains against TI's entrenched automotive analog catalogue remained the central unresolved question for AMG's growth trajectory. The platform's 2024 launch was recent enough that the first Treo-designed production programmes had not yet entered volume; the 2026–2028 ramp would test whether customers valued process-node elegance over the comfort of a supplier whose catalog had been shipping into cars for two decades.

chapters.title: From GTAT to GaN: A Chronology of Catalysts and the Forward Pipeline
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Ledger: 2021–2026

The five years between the arrival of Hassane El-Khoury and the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 produced a compressed history of strategic discontinuity — acquisitions, divestitures, a rebranding, a pair of major customer disclosures, and a technology pivot into gallium nitride — that collectively revalued ON Semiconductor from a legacy jellybean distributor into a wide-bandgap power and sensing platform. Reading the events quarter by quarter reveals a company executing a playbook at pace, while absorbing the volatility of an automotive semiconductor cycle that amplified both the drama of the ascent and the depth of the 2024–2025 trough.

**2021: Identity Crisis Resolved.** The transformation's first structural act arrived in November 2021, when onsemi closed the $415 million acquisition of GT Advanced Technologies, the Nashua, New Hampshire producer of silicon carbide crystal boules and wafers. Management described GTAT as "the final piece" of a fully vertically integrated SiC supply chain — a characterization that proved accurate as substrate scarcity throttled competitors' production schedules in 2022 and 2023. The strategic significance of vertical integration into the most constrained input in SiC manufacturing cannot be overstated: GTAT gave onsemi a defensible lead time advantage at precisely the moment EV OEM demand was accelerating. The same year, the company formally rebranded as onsemi, retiring the ON Semiconductor name and the commodity identity it carried. The lowercase logotype was marketing, but the portfolio rationalization that accompanied it — hundreds of SKUs exited, Quantenna Wi-Fi chipsets formally marked for shutdown — was operational.

**2022: Cutting Losses.** The Quantenna exit in 2022 crystallized El-Khoury's willingness to write off a predecessor's $1 billion mistake rather than defend sunk capital. Acquired in 2019 for Wi-Fi 6E exposure, Quantenna's connected-home addressable market bore no relationship to the automotive and industrial focus the new leadership was building. No buyer materialized. Onsemi shut the division, absorbed the impairment, and redeployed the engineering and capital resources toward SiC. Markets processed the exit as confirmation that the strategic narrative was genuine rather than incremental.

**2023: The Revenue Milestone and the OEM Disclosures.** Silicon carbide revenue crossing the $1 billion threshold in 2023 — against a backdrop of $8.25 billion in total company revenue at peak — validated the SiC thesis in dollar terms. The milestone arrived alongside two major customer disclosures that materially changed the Street's confidence interval around the revenue trajectory. The Vitesco Technologies supply agreement — a disclosed $1.9 billion, ten-year commitment for EliteSiC power modules — provided a visible backlog anchor. At the end of January 2023, a Volkswagen Group strategic partnership was announced, targeting supply into the MEB and PPE EV platforms. The BMW Group long-term supply agreement for next-generation traction inverter architecture followed. Together, these three European OEM relationships gave institutional investors a rare quantity: a power semiconductor company with partially contracted forward revenue.

**2025: The Trough, the Acquisition, and the Buyback.** The 2024–2025 automotive semiconductor inventory correction was the sharpest test of the transformed business model. Revenue declined from the $8.25 billion FY2023 peak to $5.995 billion in FY2025, a 27% compression over two years. Yet onsemi's non-GAAP gross margin held in the 37–38% range — far above what the pre-El-Khoury commodity mix would have sustained through a comparable volume decline — and the company generated record free cash flow of $1.42 billion on the compressed revenue base. Two strategic acts in 2025 signaled that management interpreted the trough as a buying opportunity rather than a structural break. In January, onsemi acquired Qorvo's silicon carbide JFET technology business for $118.8 million in cash, adding a switching topology with superior high-frequency performance in AI data-center power supply units — an application that had not existed as a material revenue line when El-Khoury arrived. In November, the board authorized a $6 billion share repurchase program over three years, representing approximately 12% of then-prevailing market capitalization.

**2026: GaN and the AI Pivot.** The first months of 2026 confirmed the pivot's third pillar. Q1 2026 AI data-center revenue grew more than 30% sequentially, and management guided full-year AI revenue above $500 million — implying approximately 100% year-over-year growth. Concurrently, onsemi announced a vertical GaN (vGaN) power semiconductor portfolio and signed a memorandum of understanding with Innoscience to explore foundry partnerships for lateral GaN devices. The vGaN launch extended onsemi's wide-bandgap coverage into the sub-900V switching applications where GaN outperforms SiC on switching speed and density, without requiring the company to build a proprietary GaN fab.

## The Four Re-Pricing Catalysts

Four events materially re-priced the stock against the fundamental reality that followed each move. The GTAT close in November 2021 lifted the stock sharply on the vertical-integration narrative; in retrospect, the substrate scarcity that materialized through 2022 validated the premium the market had immediately assigned. The Vitesco and Volkswagen disclosures in early-to-mid 2023 compressed the stock's risk discount on SiC revenue sustainability — the market had been treating design-win claims as aspirational, and a $1.9 billion contracted backlog changed that interpretation. The third catalyst was negative: the FY2024 and FY2025 revenue compression triggered a de-rating that at its nadir reflected little credit for the recovered SiC order book and the AI data-center opportunity. Management's interpretation was that the market was pricing onsemi as a late-cycle automotive chip company; the reality — as the Q1 2026 print demonstrated — was a business with three distinct growth vectors at different phases of their respective cycles. The fourth catalyst was the $6 billion buyback authorization in November 2025, which re-framed the stock mathematically: at 12% of market cap over three years, the authorization alone provided a return floor independent of the operating thesis.

## The Forward Catalyst Calendar: May 2026 – November 2027

| Timing | Event | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| H2 2026 | 200mm SiC wafer volume production ramp at East Fishkill | Lower per-wafer cost unlocks margin expansion and competitive pricing flexibility |
| Q3/Q4 2026 | Q2–Q4 earnings relative to $1.54–$1.64B Q2 guide | Confirms or delays the FY2026 $6.3–$6.5B revenue recovery trajectory |
| 2026 | Additional LTSA disclosures from Asian or European OEMs | Expands the contracted backlog visible to the Street; Chinese NEV OEM LTSA would be particularly re-rating |
| 2027 | Treo platform next product family launches | Demonstrates the platform's breadth beyond initial ultrasonic and AFE families; key for AMG margin |
| Ongoing | M&A — onsemi as acquirer or target | Balance sheet (net leverage <1x EBITDA) and $6B buyback suggest acquisitions are unlikely in near term; at ~$50B market cap, onsemi is a plausible target for a larger logic or analog player seeking SiC vertical integration |

## Macro Accelerators and Decelerators

The trajectory from May 2026 forward sits at the intersection of several policy and demand variables beyond onsemi's control. The EU combustion engine phase-out timeline — 2035 under current legislation but subject to political pressure from German and Italian OEM lobbying — directly determines the pace of 800V EV platform adoption in Europe, onsemi's most contracted market. Chinese NEV government subsidies, which drove the 23% sequential revenue gain from Chinese customers in Q2 2025, face uncertain renewal timelines given fiscal consolidation pressure; a subsidy rollback would pressure the fastest-growing geographic segment. US CHIPS Act funding for domestic SiC manufacturing remains a potential capital cost offset for the East Fishkill 200mm expansion, though onsemi has not publicly disclosed the status of any CHIPS application as of the frozen snapshot date. On the AI side, hyperscaler capital expenditure rates — which drove Q1 2026's 30% sequential AI data-center growth — are themselves a function of inference demand growth and large language model training schedules; any deceleration in GPU cluster buildout would slow onsemi's most recently accelerating revenue line.

## The Single Catalyst to Watch

Of the three proof points the market requires — SiC revenue recovery, AI data-center reaching the $500 million target, or gross margin sustaining above 40% — the gross margin trajectory carries the most information content. SiC revenue recovery is visible and partially contracted; the AI opportunity is growing but not yet at a scale that moves consolidated numbers. Gross margin at or above 40%, sustained across multiple quarters, would prove two simultaneous claims: that the 200mm SiC wafer transition is delivering the cost reductions management has forecasted, and that the product mix has shifted durably toward the differentiated platforms that command automotive-grade pricing premiums. A gross margin that stalls below 40% would suggest either SiC cost reduction is behind schedule or competitive pricing pressure from STMicroelectronics and Chinese domestic producers is eroding the premium. The margin line is the single number that integrates the execution of every other element of the thesis.

chapters.title: The Moat in the Crystal: IP Architecture, R&D Cadence, and Trade-Secret Framework
chapters.body:
## A Portfolio Built in Layers

onsemi's intellectual property framework is not a single fence but a layered system — patents, process trade secrets, and manufacturing know-how that compound against each other in ways that make isolated replication difficult even for well-resourced competitors. The company held several thousand issued and pending patents as of its most recent filings, covering SiC device physics, MOSFET cell architecture, epitaxial deposition chemistry, CMOS image sensor pixel design, high-dynamic-range readout circuits, and analog IC topologies within the Treo process node. But the filed patent count understates the true defensive perimeter. onsemi's vertical integration through the GTAT crystal growth operation and its captive wafer fabrication network embeds process-specific know-how in the manufacturing workforce itself — knowledge that cannot be fully disclosed in a patent application without compromising the trade secret, and that takes years of operational iteration to accumulate.

The layered structure is deliberate. Patents protect specific device geometries and circuit configurations but are time-limited and discoverable. Trade secrets — particularly the precise furnace parameters, seed preparation protocols, and dopant management recipes governing SiC crystal growth — can in principle remain proprietary indefinitely as long as physical access is controlled. The combination gives onsemi both the defensive patent thicket that large semiconductor players require for cross-licensing negotiations and a core of process trade secrets that competitors cannot design around because they cannot observe the underlying process inputs.

## R&D Investment: Sustaining the Lead Through a Revenue Trough

The financial discipline onsemi demonstrated during the 2024–2025 revenue correction did not come at the cost of R&D investment. According to the company's annual filings with the SEC, research and development expense for fiscal year 2023 was approximately $735 million, representing roughly 8.9% of the $8.25 billion in revenue recorded that year. As revenue contracted to $7.08 billion in fiscal 2024, R&D declined modestly to approximately $677 million — but the percentage of revenue rose to roughly 9.6%, signaling that management treated the expense as a floor rather than a variable cost. In fiscal 2025, with revenue declining further to approximately $6 billion, R&D approximated $610 million, sustaining the roughly 10% of revenue intensity even as gross margins were compressed by the inventory correction cycle.

The composition of that investment is as important as its magnitude. A material share of SiC-specific R&D has been directed at the 200mm wafer transition at the East Fishkill, New York facility — a capital-intensive and technically demanding program to produce SiC substrates at the same wafer diameter as silicon, which would reduce per-die cost by 40% to 50% relative to 150mm production. The next-generation EliteSiC MOSFET device architecture — incorporating JFET integration and targeting sub-100-nanosecond switching transitions for AI data-center power supply unit applications — represents a parallel engineering track. On the ISG side, R&D resources have been directed at global-shutter architectures for factory automation vision, near-infrared (NIR) and short-wave infrared (SWIR) sensor development for industrial inspection, and the high-dynamic-range pixel designs that differentiate onsemi's automotive image sensors in ADAS surround-view applications.

## Treo as Platform IP: Multiplying Returns on a Single Process Investment

The Treo analog platform represents a qualitatively different form of IP than the individual device patents in onsemi's portfolio. Where a device patent protects a single product configuration for a fixed term, a proprietary process node creates a recurring design advantage across every product family subsequently developed on that process. onsemi's 65-nanometer bulk CMOS with drain-extended DMOS (BCD) process — developed internally and not available on standard commercial foundry menus — supports operating voltages from 1 to 90 volts and junction temperatures to 175°C, parameters matched to the thermal and electrical demands of automotive ADAS sensor fusion, industrial motor control, and high-density data-center power management.

The strategic logic is that each new Treo-derived product — ultrasonic park-assist sensors, multi-phase PWM controllers, precision LDOs, LED drivers — requires no incremental investment in the underlying process, only in the circuit design layer. The process knowledge is retained inside onsemi's manufacturing organization regardless of competitive design activity. Competitors without access to the Treo node cannot replicate Treo-derived products by reverse-engineering the silicon, because the process itself is proprietary and the foundry infrastructure to reproduce it does not exist externally. This platform model closely parallels the design leverage Texas Instruments extracts from its own proprietary BCD process families — and represents a conscious strategic choice by El-Khoury to compete on manufacturing differentiation rather than on catalog breadth alone.

## The SiC Patent Landscape and Cross-Licensing Reality

onsemi operates in a SiC patent landscape populated by large and aggressive IP holders. STMicroelectronics — which held approximately 35% global SiC market share through 2025 — has been building a SiC patent portfolio since the early 2000s, as has Infineon through its CoolSiC program and through the Siltectra cold-split wafer technology acquisition. The practical consequence is that freedom-to-operate in SiC MOSFETs almost certainly requires cross-licensing agreements among the major participants. onsemi has not disclosed specific cross-licensing terms in its public filings, but the absence of litigation among the three leading Western SiC suppliers is consistent with an informal or formal cross-licensing regime in which large patent portfolios function primarily as defensive instruments that enable negotiated access rather than exclusion. The greater patent litigation risk historically has involved smaller entrants or patent assertion entities challenging device-specific claims — a risk onsemi manages through its own portfolio breadth.

## GTAT: The Trade Secret at the Foundation

The most strategically irreplaceable IP asset in onsemi's portfolio cannot be read in any patent filing. The proprietary Kayex and Quantum crystal growth furnace technology acquired with GTAT in November 2021 — along with the process parameters refined over thousands of growth runs in Hudson, New Hampshire — constitutes the foundation of onsemi's SiC substrate supply advantage. The specific combination of furnace geometry, seed crystal preparation, temperature gradient management, and source powder purity that determines whether a 150mm or 200mm boule achieves the defect density required for device-grade wafers is a matter of empirical process engineering accumulated over years. These parameters are not fully patentable — disclosing them in a patent application would allow competitors to reproduce them — and so they are protected primarily as trade secrets, with access restricted to a small population of process engineers operating within secured manufacturing environments.

The competitive significance is difficult to overstate. SiC substrate supply constraints limited every major SiC device manufacturer's ability to ramp production throughout the 2022–2024 period. onsemi's internal crystal growth eliminates this bottleneck for its own device programs and, unlike a wafer purchase agreement, cannot be interrupted by a supplier's competing commercial priorities. The GTAT process know-how is, in this sense, the moat within the moat — the IP layer beneath the patents that competitors cannot acquire through licensing negotiations or design-around engineering.

chapters.title: Six Structural Risks: From SiC Competition to China Concentration to Balance Sheet Discipline
chapters.body:
## The SiC Price War That Has Yet to Arrive

The most structurally consequential risk facing onsemi is not cyclical — it is competitive. STMicroelectronics held roughly 35% of the silicon carbide power device market as of the frozen window, a position it had built through decade-long investment in Catania-based SiC wafer manufacturing and entrenched European OEM relationships, particularly with Stellantis and Renault. Infineon's CoolSiC product line was scaling aggressively at its Villach, Austria fab. And a cohort of Chinese domestic producers — SICC, Sanan Optoelectronics, and TankeBlue — were progressing down the manufacturing cost curve with the explicit backing of Chinese industrial policy, serving an NEV market that represented onsemi's fastest-growing customer cluster.

The risk is not that onsemi loses design wins. The more probable mechanism is ASP compression: as aggregate SiC wafer supply expands across these multiple competing production lines, spot pricing pressure migrates toward long-term agreement pricing, eroding the revenue per inverter that has underpinned onsemi's non-GAAP gross margin recovery. A 10% decline in SiC ASPs across a revenue base where SiC-related PSG content accounts for an estimated $1.5–$1.8 billion of onsemi's FY2026 run-rate implies a top-line headwind of $150–$180 million annually. At onsemi's current non-GAAP gross margin structure of 38.4% — and assuming SiC products carry above-average gross margins closer to 45% given automotive qualification premiums — the gross profit impact of a 10–15% price decline sustained over three years would compress reported group gross margins by approximately 150–250 basis points, narrowing the envelope from the current 38–39% range toward 36–37%. Vertical integration provides a partial but incomplete buffer: controlling crystal growth through the GTAT Hudson, New Hampshire facility reduces substrate input costs by an estimated 20–30% relative to spot SiC wafer pricing, but does not eliminate the impact of device-level ASP compression in customer negotiations.

The management response to this risk has been twofold: locking revenue under long-term supply agreements — Vitesco's disclosed $1.9 billion, 10-year commitment being the most prominent — and expanding into higher-value SiC topologies, including the $118.8 million Qorvo JFET acquisition completed in January 2025. JFETs command a premium over standard MOSFETs in AI data-center PSU applications, providing a partial ASP offset if commodity SiC MOSFET pricing softens.

## The EV Cycle as a Two-Edged Sword

The inventory correction that drove onsemi's revenue from the $8,252.4 million peak in fiscal 2023 to $5,995.4 million in fiscal 2025 was, in management's characterization, a temporary digestion of excess automotive semiconductor stock accumulated during the post-COVID supply chain disruption. The thesis of cyclical recovery rested on the underlying secular growth in EV production volumes eventually reasserting itself. But structural uncertainty surrounds that baseline.

European combustion-engine phase-out timelines were under legislative pressure as of the frozen window, with political coalitions in Germany and Italy pushing to soften the 2035 new-ICE ban. Consumer price sensitivity — particularly in Western markets where average EV transaction prices exceeded $50,000 — continued to constrain mass-market EV adoption rates. Charging infrastructure gaps in Southern and Eastern Europe further dampened fleet conversion rates among small-business and commercial buyers.

A 20% downside scenario to consensus EV production forecasts through FY2027 is not implausible in a base case where European policy softens and North American consumer demand plateaus. Modelling this risk against onsemi's current revenue trajectory: if EV-exposed SiC revenue represents approximately 25–30% of onsemi's FY2026 guided run-rate ($6.3–$6.5 billion implied by Q2 2026 guidance midpoint), a 20% demand-driven haircut translates to a $315–$390 million annualised revenue shortfall. At the company's current non-GAAP operating margin profile of approximately 18–20%, that volume reduction — assuming limited offsetting cost reduction given the fixed-cost intensity of vertically integrated SiC manufacturing — would reduce non-GAAP operating income by $60–$80 million, or approximately $0.16–$0.22 per diluted share on the current share count. For FY2027, where sell-side consensus had embedded meaningful SiC revenue recovery, the EPS risk from this scenario is larger: potentially $0.40–$0.55 per share against a consensus EPS estimate in the $3.50–$4.00 range.

## AI Revenue Concentration and Design-Win Volatility

Management guided FY2026 AI data-center revenue above $500 million — an approximately 100% year-over-year growth rate that, if achieved, would represent the single largest revenue growth vector in the company's portfolio. Q1 2026 AI revenue grew more than 30% sequentially, validating early-stage momentum. The risk embedded in this narrative is customer concentration and design-cycle discontinuity.

Hyperscaler GPU cluster build-outs are driven by procurement decisions made by a small number of infrastructure engineering teams. A pause or deferral in AI infrastructure capital expenditure — whether driven by efficiency improvements in inference-side GPU utilisation, interest rate sensitivity in technology capital budgets, or regulatory friction in data-centre permitting — would disproportionately affect a supplier with $500 million in revenue concentrated across three to five buyers. Unlike the long-term supply agreements that provide automotive SiC revenue with multi-year backlog visibility, AI data-centre power conversion procurement operates on shorter design-win cycles tied to rack architecture generations. As GPU rack power requirements evolve rapidly from 400W to 1,000W-plus per accelerator card, onsemi must continuously re-win design-in positions in each new PSU generation rather than relying on locked-in commitments. The FY2026 guidance implies confidence in current design wins; it does not guarantee FY2027 re-win rates.

## Sony's Long Shadow Over the Image Sensor Segment

onsemi's Intelligent Sensing Group represented the company's highest-margin business segment, benefiting from global leadership in automotive CMOS image sensors built around the South Portland, Maine wafer fabrication facility. Sony Semiconductor Solutions — the global CMOS image sensor leader with an estimated 45–50% share of the overall image sensor market — had been publicly increasing investment in automotive-specific sensor architectures as of the frozen window.

Sony's competitive pressure operates on a lagged timeline. Automotive sensor design-wins typically translate to vehicle programmes with three-to-five-year development cycles, meaning Sony's current investment would not materially affect onsemi's ISG revenue until the FY2028–FY2030 range. In the near term, onsemi's installed base of surround-view and ADAS front-camera wins across BMW, Volkswagen, and Hyundai-KIA platforms provides meaningful protection. But the existence of a well-capitalised, technically credible competitor with existing relationships across the same tier-1 camera module integrators represents a structural ceiling on onsemi's pricing power in ISG renewal cycles. If Sony captures 5–8 percentage points of onsemi's current automotive image sensor share over a five-year horizon, the ISG revenue and margin impact would be material — potentially $200–$300 million in annual ISG revenue at risk by FY2030.

## The China Bilateral and Manufacturing Footprint

China revenue grew 23% sequentially in Q2 2025, driven by accelerating ramp volumes among domestic NEV OEMs and their tier-1 inverter suppliers. This trajectory is valuable — and fragile. onsemi's manufacturing footprint is geographically distributed across the United States, Czech Republic, Slovakia, South Korea, Malaysia, and the Philippines, but its revenue exposure to China is concentrated in sales rather than production, creating an asymmetric tariff risk. An escalation of US-China export controls on advanced semiconductor equipment — potentially affecting the 200mm SiC wafer fab expansion at East Fishkill — or a retaliatory tariff regime targeting US semiconductor companies selling into the Chinese NEV market could simultaneously impair both capital investment plans and revenue. China likely represents 15–20% of onsemi's automotive semiconductor revenue at the frozen window. A scenario of sharply reduced China market access — not complete exclusion but a 30–40% revenue decline in that geography — would reduce total company revenue by $250–$350 million annually and compress already-thin margins given the fixed-cost base.

## The Buyback Promise and the Quantenna Warning

The $6 billion three-year buyback authorization announced in November 2025 was presented as a signal of management's conviction in the stock's undervaluation and the company's long-term earnings power. The arithmetic is tight but credible: FY2025 free cash flow of $1,418.6 million — a 24.0% FCF margin on $5,995.4 million in revenue — demonstrates the capital efficiency of the transformed business model. If revenue recovers toward $7–$8 billion over three years and FCF margins are maintained above 20%, annual FCF generation of $1.4–$1.6 billion implies approximately $4.2–$4.8 billion in cumulative FCF over the buyback window. Completing a $6 billion authorization at that pace would require either modest leverage or modest shortfall versus the full authorization — both manageable.

The constraint is execution risk, not authorization size. onsemi's history carries one cautionary data point. The Quantenna Communications acquisition, executed for approximately $1 billion in June 2019 under prior CEO Keith Jackson, was subsequently judged to be a strategic misalignment with the automotive and industrial focus El-Khoury articulated upon arrival in December 2020. The division was shut down in 2022 with a full write-off. A transformative acquisition at an analogous scale — $1–$2 billion — would consume one to two years of FCF, mechanically deferring buyback execution and potentially resetting shareholder confidence in the capital return commitment. Management has not indicated any acquisition pipeline as of the frozen window, and the Qorvo JFET deal at $118.8 million exemplifies the bolt-on-only discipline El-Khoury has maintained. But the Quantenna precedent establishes that the board and management team were not immune, under prior leadership, to overpriced strategic bets. Whether the current team's discipline is structural or situational remains, in the absence of a test case, an open question for investors underwriting the buyback narrative.

chapters.title: The Execution Test: onsemi's Quarter-by-Quarter Catalyst Map Through May 2027
chapters.body:
## The Stakes After the Inflection

The story onsemi told through 2025 was a story of endurance: margins held, free cash flow reached a record $1.42 billion, and the company spent every dollar of it buying back its own stock while waiting for the automotive semiconductor inventory correction to clear. The story that begins in Q2 2026 is a different kind of story — an execution test. The thesis is now widely understood on the sell side, the AI data-center narrative has driven an approximate 90 percent year-to-date share price rally from early 2026 lows, and the stock trades at roughly $131–$135 per share, implying a market capitalization near $50 billion. The question investors are pricing is no longer whether Hassane El-Khoury's transformation was real. It is whether onsemi can deliver four consecutive quarters of re-acceleration — in revenue, in margin, and in the two revenue lines that matter most — against a backdrop of European EV registration uncertainty, Chinese NEV price wars, and hyperscaler CapEx cycles that remain opaque quarter to quarter.

## Q2 2026: The First Real Test

When onsemi reported Q1 2026 results in late April, management issued Q2 2026 guidance that was specific enough to define clear success and failure thresholds. Revenue guidance spanned $1,540 million to $1,640 million, a midpoint of $1,590 million. Non-GAAP gross margin was guided to 37.4 percent to 39.4 percent — a wide band that management attributed to product mix uncertainty as AI data-center revenue scaled. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was guided to $0.65 to $0.77.

> "We expect Q2 2026 revenue of $1,540 million to $1,640 million, with non-GAAP gross margins of 37.4 percent to 39.4 percent and non-GAAP EPS of $0.65 to $0.77."

The Q2 earnings release is expected in late July 2026. A beat requires revenue above $1,600 million — above the guidance midpoint — and non-GAAP gross margin above 39.0 percent, which would represent a meaningful step toward the 40 percent threshold that analysts view as the re-rating catalyst. A miss is defined either by revenue falling below the $1,540 million floor, which would suggest the automotive recovery is stalling rather than accelerating, or by gross margin declining sequentially from the 38.5 percent recorded in Q1 2026 — a signal that AI data-center product mix is dilutive rather than accretive to margins in its current ramp phase. Sell-side consensus for Q2 2026 revenue sits in the $1,580–$1,640 million range, clustering around the midpoint, with non-GAAP EPS consensus near $0.70–$0.72.

Product catalysts to monitor heading into the Q2 call include any update on the 200mm SiC wafer fabrication ramp at East Fishkill. Management has described the 200mm transition as a cost reduction lever — 200mm SiC wafers carry meaningfully lower cost per die than 150mm — and any disclosed timeline acceleration or customer qualification milestone would be a positive read-through to 2027 and 2028 gross margin targets.

## Q3 2026: The H2 Proof Point

Management's qualitative FY2026 guidance was explicit that second-half revenue should outgrow first half. With implied H1 2026 revenue near $3.1 billion (Q1 at $1,513 million plus Q2 at the guidance midpoint of $1,590 million), the H2 outgrowth commitment implies H2 2026 revenue above $3.1 billion. That positions Q3 2026 consensus revenue in the $1,650–$1,700 million range, rising toward $1,700–$1,800 million in Q4.

A Q3 beat requires continued sequential revenue growth — any deceleration from Q2 to Q3 would contradict the management narrative — and non-GAAP gross margin sustained above 39 percent. The Q3 results are expected in late October or early November 2026.

The macro data points that will frame the Q3 setup are consequential and observable in real time. European EV registrations for July and August 2026, released monthly by the European Automobile Manufacturers Association, will signal whether the BMW and Volkswagen SiC ramps are tracking to plan. China NEV sales data from the China Passenger Car Association — available monthly — will indicate whether the sequential growth in onsemi's Chinese customer revenue that began in Q2 2025 is continuing. On the AI side, CapEx commentary from Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta in their respective Q2 2026 earnings calls (which will print in late July and early August 2026, weeks before onsemi's own Q3 reporting) will either confirm or challenge the trajectory toward onsemi's $500 million AI data-center FY2026 target.

Investor events in the September–October 2026 window typically include Deutsche Bank's Technology Conference and the Evercore ISI Semiconductor Summit — both venues where management has historically updated the SiC design-win pipeline and AI data-center revenue trajectory between formal earnings calls.

## The Five Numbers That Define the Re-Rating

Across the next four quarters, five metrics will function as the most reliable leading and lagging indicators of whether onsemi's transformation thesis is being validated in financial results.

The first is **SiC revenue as an absolute figure or as a percentage of total revenue**. onsemi does not break out SiC revenue as a standalone line item in its formal segment reporting, but management has discussed it in qualitative terms on earnings calls. Any disclosure of SiC revenue exceeding 25 percent of total revenue — implying roughly $1.5 billion on a $6 billion annualized run-rate — would represent a significant milestone confirming that the EV traction inverter ramp is real.

The second is **AI data-center revenue's quarterly progression toward the $500 million-plus FY2026 target**. With Q1 2026 representing more than 30 percent sequential growth, investors are working backward from the annual target to estimate quarterly run-rates. A Q4 2026 quarterly contribution of $150 million or more would put the annual figure on track.

The third is **non-GAAP gross margin trajectory toward 40 percent**. The non-GAAP gross margin recovered from a trough near 37.6 percent in Q2 2025 to 38.5 percent in Q1 2026. Each 50 basis points of sequential improvement compresses the distance to the 40 percent threshold that management has implicitly targeted. A Q4 2026 print above 40 percent would represent a meaningful milestone and is the single variable most correlated to sell-side price target revisions.

The fourth is **diluted share count reduction**. The $6 billion buyback authorization announced in November 2025 — roughly three-year duration — implies roughly $2 billion per year of repurchase activity. With the stock trading near $130–$135 per share, each quarter's buyback should reduce diluted share count by roughly 3–4 million shares. Consistent execution is both an EPS accretion mechanism and a signal of management's conviction in the stock's intrinsic value.

The fifth is **backlog and book-to-bill commentary on earnings calls**. Management's language around order linearity is a leading indicator of six-to-nine months' demand. Language affirming that design-win pull-through is accelerating — particularly from Chinese NEV OEMs and from AI server ODMs — would provide forward visibility into the Q4 2026 and Q1 2027 revenue trajectory.

## The Bull and Bear Into Q4 2026

| Scenario | SiC Revenue | AI Data-Center | Gross Margin | Multiple | Stock Implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | Re-accelerates; EV OEM inventory fully digests by Q3 | Reaches $150M+ in Q4 2026; FY2026 target met | Exits 2026 above 40% | 26–28x forward non-GAAP EPS (~$2.80) | Stock re-rates toward $70–$80 range |
| **Bear** | EV demand disappoints in H2; China macro softens | Plateaus below $100M/quarter; FY target missed | Stalls at 38–39%; mix headwinds persist | Compresses to 18–20x | Multiple de-rating offsets earnings growth |

The bull case rests on the convergence of three cycles simultaneously inflecting upward: the European and Korean automotive SiC ramp, which is scheduled but not yet fully in production; the Chinese NEV supply chain deepening its onsemi content as domestic SiC competitors remain capacity-constrained at scale; and the AI data-center power conversion ramp reaching sufficient quarterly revenue to be visible as a standalone growth vector. In this scenario, onsemi exits 2026 with gross margin above 40 percent and non-GAAP EPS on a trajectory toward $3.00–$3.50 for FY2027, supporting a re-rating to 26–28x forward earnings.

The bear case requires only one of those three cycles to disappoint materially. EV demand in Europe has been sensitive to subsidy policy changes, and any rollback of purchase incentives in Germany or France would delay the OEM ramp timelines underwriting the SiC revenue recovery. AI data-center revenue, while growing rapidly, remains concentrated in a small number of hyperscaler relationships and could plateau if CapEx allocation shifts toward compute rather than power infrastructure. If gross margin stalls at 38–39 percent — still materially above the pre-transformation floor, but below the threshold needed to justify the current multiple — the stock's 26x trailing non-GAAP earnings could compress toward 18–20x, erasing much of the year's rally even as underlying earnings hold steady.

The calendar through Q1 2027 will resolve that uncertainty quarter by quarter, one earnings print at a time.

chapters.title: 2026–2030: The Long Arc of Electrification, AI Infrastructure, and onsemi's Positioning
chapters.body:
## Three Vectors, One Thesis

The five years from 2026 to 2030 represent, in management's framing and in the architecture of the product portfolio El-Khoury assembled, the compound phase — the period when the three strategic bets placed between 2021 and 2024 begin to pay simultaneously rather than sequentially. Silicon carbide content per vehicle rises as 800V architectures displace 400V across European and Korean OEM platforms. Automotive image sensors migrate from one-megapixel surround-view arrays to four- and eight-megapixel perception stacks as ADAS systems advance toward Level 3 conditional automation. And the power density of AI data-center racks escalates past 100 kilowatts, demanding power conversion hardware that only wide-bandgap semiconductors can efficiently provide. Each vector compounds the others: the same El-Khoury-era investments in SiC vertical integration, image sensor process technology, and the Treo analog platform provide the common substrate.

The arithmetic of the SiC market alone is striking. Industry research houses estimated the global SiC power device market at approximately $3–4 billion in 2024, concentrated in automotive traction inverters and onboard chargers but expanding rapidly into industrial motor drives and server power supplies. The consensus projection by 2030 is $10–15 billion — a three-to-four-fold expansion over six years, driven primarily by the structural increase in SiC device count per vehicle as 800V battery architectures become mainstream and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles extend their electric range toward 100 miles, a threshold that creates a compelling economic case for SiC in the PHEV OBC. At onsemi's approximately 25 percent market share — established through the Vitesco $1.9 billion, 10-year supply agreement, BMW's next-generation traction platform, Volkswagen's MEB and PPE commitments, and Hyundai's E-GMP design wins — the implied SiC revenue in 2030 ranges from $2.5 billion to $3.75 billion. Against an estimated $1 billion in SiC revenue at the 2025 trough, this represents a 2.5-to-4-times revenue expansion from a single product family within a single segment.

## The 200mm Inflection

The mechanism that makes that expansion financially compelling rather than merely topline-enhancing is the transition from 150mm to 200mm SiC wafers — the single most important manufacturing event in onsemi's 2026–2028 roadmap. A 200mm wafer increases the number of usable die per wafer by approximately 78 percent relative to a 150mm wafer, which translates — accounting for edge loss and yield improvements at larger diameter — into an estimated 30 to 40 percent reduction in the cost of goods per SiC device. At the East Fishkill, New York fab, which onsemi acquired from GlobalFoundries in 2023 and retrofitted for 200mm SiC production, management has indicated volume ramp in the second half of 2026 progressing toward full commercial production through 2027.

The competitive significance of this timing is substantial. STMicroelectronics, which holds the leading approximately 35 percent share in SiC power devices, and Infineon Technologies, whose CoolSiC MOSFET family competes directly with onsemi's EliteSiC, are both pursuing their own 200mm transitions on broadly similar timelines. The race is not a winner-take-all event — all three incumbents are likely to reach 200mm volume production within roughly 18 to 24 months of each other — but the company that achieves sustained 200mm yield fastest will have the clearest pathway to competing on price for automotive design wins without sacrificing gross margin. For onsemi, the GTAT-derived internal crystal growth capability at Hudson, New Hampshire provides a supply-chain advantage that neither STM nor Infineon replicates fully: substrate availability, not wafer fab capacity, has historically been the binding constraint on SiC production ramps, and controlling the boule-to-wafer supply chain insulates onsemi from the substrate spot-market dynamics that have disrupted pure-play wafer purchasers in prior cycles.

## Image Sensing's Escalating Revenue Per Vehicle

The second compounding vector is quieter in analyst discourse but structurally durable. Automotive ADAS architectures advancing from Level 2 — lane-keeping, adaptive cruise — to Level 3 conditional automation and eventually Level 4 require not merely more cameras but higher-resolution, higher-frame-rate, higher-dynamic-range cameras capable of supporting onboard neural-network inference at the sensor level. A typical Level 2 surround-view system deployed in a mid-2020s OEM platform uses eight cameras averaging one to two megapixels. A Level 3 platform targeted for the late 2020s requires the equivalent of twelve to sixteen cameras averaging four to eight megapixels, with global-shutter architectures for motion clarity and high dynamic range for low-light performance. Each step up the resolution ladder and frame-rate ladder represents incremental ISG revenue per vehicle — onsemi's position as the largest automotive image sensor supplier globally means it captures a disproportionate share of every dollar of ADAS content increase across European, Korean, and North American OEMs. The South Portland, Maine wafer fabrication facility, the primary manufacturing site for ISG image sensors, carries a relatively stable capacity base — ISG does not face the same greenfield capex requirements as SiC — making incremental revenue from ADAS camera upgrades highly accretive to segment margin.

## AI Data Centers as the Third Pillar

The third vector emerged as a structural story only in 2025, but its growth rate has been the most dramatic. Management guided FY2026 AI data-center revenue above $500 million — implying roughly 100 percent year-over-year growth — against a backdrop in which Q1 2026 AI revenue grew more than 30 percent sequentially. The mechanism is architectural: as GPU compute per rack escalates past 100 kilowatts, hyperscaler and ODM power architects migrate away from 12V server bus architectures toward 48V and 400V intermediate bus designs, where SiC and gallium nitride devices outperform silicon in efficiency density. The January 2025 acquisition of Qorvo's SiC JFET technology for $118.8 million extended the EliteSiC portfolio into the high-frequency AC-DC conversion segment where switching losses at silicon's limits impose an efficiency ceiling that is architecturally unacceptable for liquid-cooled GPU clusters.

## The GaN Option

The vGaN program and the Innoscience GaN foundry memorandum of understanding announced in 2026 represent something between genuine strategic optionality and a well-constructed hedge. GaN on silicon outperforms SiC below approximately 900V and at switching frequencies above 100 kilohertz — parameters that describe the onboard charger application precisely. Some analysts have projected GaN displacing SiC in OBC applications on a 2027–2029 horizon as GaN cost curves decline faster than SiC. If that scenario materializes, onsemi's vGaN portfolio — delivered through a combination of internal development and the Innoscience foundry relationship, without requiring a new owned GaN fab — would allow the PSG segment to defend the OBC revenue stream rather than cede it to GaN-native competitors such as Navitas Semiconductor or Power Integrations. The degree to which vGaN represents a primary growth driver versus a defensive hedge remains an open question; the capital-light foundry-partner model suggests management views GaN as insurance rather than a core investment thesis.

## The Margin Architecture

The financial architecture of the 2026–2030 period, as management has framed it, converges on a specific trajectory: non-GAAP gross margins expanding above the 38–39 percent range recovered in early 2026, toward 40–43 percent by FY2028 as the product mix continues to tilt toward high-ASP SiC and image sensor revenue and the 200mm cost reduction flows through the income statement. On $8–9 billion of revenue — approximately where sell-side consensus models converge for FY2028 — a 40–43 percent non-GAAP gross margin implies $3.2–3.9 billion of gross profit, and at the non-GAAP operating margin levels the company has demonstrated at prior revenue peaks, non-GAAP operating income of $2.0–2.5 billion becomes structurally achievable. Against FY2025 non-GAAP operating income of approximately $1.1 billion, that would represent a near-doubling of operating earnings. With the $6 billion buyback program reducing diluted share count materially through 2028, non-GAAP EPS well above $5 on a contracted share base is a mathematically coherent scenario.

## Risk: The Variables That Could Break the Arc

The bull case is coherent; it is not guaranteed. The 2026–2030 outlook rests on a global EV adoption trajectory that has already proven susceptible to interest-rate environments, OEM pricing pressure, and charging infrastructure constraints that decelerate adoption curves. The Chinese NEV market, which provided 23 percent sequential revenue growth in Q2 2025 and represents onsemi's fastest-growing customer cluster, is simultaneously the market where domestic SiC producers — BYD's in-house semiconductor arm, Silan Microelectronics, SICC — are investing most aggressively in capacity. If Chinese domestic SiC suppliers achieve competitive parity with foreign incumbents in the 2027–2029 timeframe, the addressable market for onsemi in China contracts to the portion of Chinese NEV production sold through OEMs with mandates favoring internationally qualified suppliers — a meaningful but shrinking share of the total.

The competitive pressure from STMicroelectronics and Infineon is structural rather than episodic. STM has invested heavily in SiC substrate sourcing through its Norstel acquisition and joint ventures; Infineon's CoolSiC program benefits from the company's industrial-application installed base and European OEM relationships. A scenario where European OEMs — BMW, Volkswagen, Stellantis — diversify SiC sourcing more evenly across the three major incumbents would compress onsemi's share below 25 percent at the same time the total market is expanding, producing revenue growth but margin pressure as average selling prices normalize in a more competitive supply environment.

The bear case — Chinese domestic SiC crowding out onsemi in Asia, European OEM share splitting more evenly among the three incumbents, and AI data-center power demand proving more volatile than hyperscaler capex commentary implies — could resolve into a company generating $7.0–7.5 billion in revenue with mid-30s gross margins by 2028 rather than the $9 billion, 40-plus percent margin bull case. That outcome, while significantly below the aspirational model, would still represent a structurally superior business to the 2019 commodity-component onsemi — and it would have been built, deliberately, by a CEO who understood that the highest-risk path was standing still.
